en: Prefaces to the Twelve Kinds of Scripture Readings by Master Lingting Regarding the twelve kinds of scripture readings composed by the Great Master Lingting: are they words? Or are they wordless?

If one considers them wordless, then even a torrential flow of eloquence has already been heard by all. If one considers them words, then since the Dharma is fundamentally without dharma, how could there be words?

This is a common expression of gratitude. Nevertheless, when Bodhidharma came from the West, he did not establish written words; when Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma, the heavenly maidens scattered flowers.
Within silence there was speech, and within speech there was silence. Master Ling, pitying the overgrown thickets of those who study at the end of the tradition, [has composed this work].

Those of high caliber hunt the void; those of low caliber merely follow rote memorization. How does this compare to one who mirrors the origins and developments of the teachings, clarifies doubtful points, and reflects upon them with earnest concern?
Therefore, in reading various sections of the scriptures, I have not hesitated to expose their depths for the sake of providing a ferry and raft for the world. My words state:
"Yunxi, being constrained by necessity, could not avoid defiling the ancients. Inferring from this intent, was it a fondness for disputation? —The Tripitaka Master.
The scriptural teachings are the words spoken by the sages of the Western Regions out of necessity.
Master Yunxi has likewise spoken these words out of necessity after having read twelve kinds of sutras. Long ago, our Confucius lamented that the subtle words were about to perish;
he withdrew and, together with his seventy disciples, cultivated and clarified the Way of the former kings, editing the *Shi*, *Shu*, and establishing the *Li*.
He delighted in transmitting these teachings to posterity, so that the meanings of the Six Classics thereafter became as brilliant as the sun and moon and as vast as the flowing rivers.
Master Ling was truly a disciple of our Confucius; his perusal of the scriptures was characterized by transparency and tirelessness, which remains consistent with the will of Confucius.
As for the sealing of the mouth at Vaiśālī and the closing of the room at Magadha—these were instances where the function of the teaching’s pivot was perfectly realized.

"Originating from the same source and following the same thread, when Master Ling heard him discourse on the sutras, those who were dull-witted found their jaws agape with understanding, while those who were eloquent rolled back their tongues in silence.
The *Qinglong* commentaries and sub-commentaries could well have been burned; was he speaking when silent, or silent when speaking?
Though he employed various indirect analogies among the twelve types of teaching, it was simply a matter of 'not establishing words. As Master Xizhai said: Ling..."
Whether speaking horizontally or vertically, deeply or superficially, there is nothing he does not speak; yet, in the ultimate sense, there is not a single thing spoken.
Were it not for one who possesses profound insight, how could Master Ling dare to express this?
On the Mid-Autumn Festival of the Gengxu year, the ninth year of the Kangxi era, his dharma-brother Yang Yongjian inscribed this at Jingshengtang in Wulin.
Regarding the twelve types of sutra commentaries reviewed by Master Lingting:
Yaoshan’s “Reading Sutras” was intended merely to shield his eyes; Qing Huayan’s recitation of the *Lotus Sutra* was likewise a practice of later, eminent figures.
How could it be that only the Elder of Taiyuan was skilled at explaining the three causes, while the junior master Jingyin alone was versed in the five teachings?
Master Lingting was originally a renowned sage of Jiangzuo who transmitted the orthodox lineage of Dongshan;

there is no fundamental tenet of the five houses that he did not explore to its subtle depths and exhaust its source, discussing their similarities and differences. Furthermore, he annotated the scriptures of the Tripitaka and composed literary works through his insightful exegesis, as follows:
The Chan of the ancestral masters who came [to China] forms a single thread. People today, however, possess shallow understanding and fail to discern the complete scripture;

they move about saying that it is merely a heap of old paper, needlessly laboring over its selection. They do not realize that when the World-Honored One ascended the seat, Kāśyapa broke into a smile;

that before Mount Kukkuṭapāda, every beat of the drum is the command. When the bannerpole is toppled, one exchanges it for the eyes; the transmission from the palm-leaf manuscripts has been overturned.

It turns the nostrils upside down. Were it not for one who is proficient in both the doctrine (*zong*) and the teaching (*shuo*), how could one possibly raise both the "knocking" and the "singing" together?

This compilation consists of twelve types; through manifold transformations, it produces wonders without end. Sometimes it relies on the teachings to clarify the doctrine; sometimes it cites Confucianism to enter into Buddhism.
Thus, it causes the Yellow-Faced Gautama to lower his clouds and join the procession by the side of the Caoxi Road, seizing the market.

A whole class of pedantic scholars—Cao, Liu, Yan, Xie, Pan, Lu, Xu, and Geng—can do nothing but swallow their breath and stifle their voices, crawling before Mount Ling and prostrating themselves in unison.
Now, should one say they possess words, or that they are without words?
Whether Confucian, Buddhist, or Taoist, this is truly a book that has never existed since the beginning of time;
it is certainly an unalterable classic within the land of China. Having traveled three thousand li, one must not fail to mention it when meeting others.

Preface to the Twelve Kinds of Scriptures Read by the Venerable Lingting of Yunxi, inscribed by the Daoist Renunciant Li Yuankuan of Boyuan, the Thirty-fifth Generation of the Zhengzong (Orthodox Lineage) of Cao-Dong, of Yuzhang.

The White Horse has newly translated [the scriptures], and the Golden Wheel has just begun to turn. The Brahma-sounds from Mount Yu have transmitted a transcendent style surpassing that of the Huangchu era; Zhi Dun...
Pure discourse fanned a gentle breeze over Jiangzuo; passing through the forests of Mount Lu, he sought the Way, yet his vision was hazy and difficult to rely upon.

Entering Waguan Temple to exhaustively study the scriptures, he hesitated and could not turn back. Need one necessarily see the West on the peaks of Songyun before the meaning of the Patriarchs becomes clear in the halls of Emperor Wu of Liang?
Some might say that the five thousand scrolls are nothing but a mass of clouds and mist.

The three hundred palace courtyards all belong to the domain of the physical body. If this were so, then Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna would not have been worthy successors at the gateway of the Shaoshi [Mount Song] school;
and Asanga and Vasubandhu should have abandoned the Śītavana and the Trāyastriṃśa heavens long ago.

To block the source of the Yellow River while dredging the Luo tributary, or to bury the Celestial Pillar while sealing the Bo and Min mountains—such would not be a correct approach to discourse. (Ling)

Master Ting has returned once more to Vulture Peak; he manifests his traces within the Bamboo Grove. Commanding all according to his will, he drives the azure cocks and yellow horses beyond the twin trees.
Forgetting emotion in his coming and going, he inscribes green characters and vermilion texts outside the Bimbasāra Cave.

When the fire-jewels soar and blaze, the dragon-patterns of the ocean treasury shine forth; when the pure brocade flows like rosy clouds, the palace of the makaras is filled with the fragrance of the great phoenixes.

Fierce! His discourse on doctrine reached even the most subtle nuances; his exegesis of the sutras occasionally paused at the number twelve. He questioned the Hu monks regarding the iron alms-bowl; he summoned those of equal rank to invite them.
He sent the scholars running in their sedan chairs as they hastened toward him upon hearing the wind of his reputation; they prostrated themselves in worship.

By the side of the pond, the divine maidens supported his desk and inkstone while dew moistened their pearl pouches; in the heavens, the numinous deities attended upon him as the wind stirred the Tiger Hall. Formerly, in Dingzhou—
The Way prizes the transmission of truth, inscribing it upon the adamantine; Touzi’s reputation is lofty, gathering the echoes of his voice from Mahābodhi.

Meeting Dushun, the waters and mists turn back; facing Langye, the mountains and rivers perform a dance. One thus knows that by the side of the *khaṭvāṅga* pillar, the *kaṣāya* of Kukkutapāda remains;
within the Jeta Grove, the robes and bowl of Dayu are hung. As for those who are fragmented and scattered...

They have drowned themselves in fishing traps and snares; they have abandoned the ropes and slips of those who passed before. They take delight in the resonance of flutes and pipes for their ears and eyes, yet when asked about the pitch-pipes (*lülǚ*), they cannot distinguish the methods of Linglun. They apply vermilion and ochre to their steps and courtyards, yet when pressed regarding the patterns of *fǔ* and *fú*, they do not know black from white. Is this to treat a single sandal as a straw carriage, or to take a yellow plum as a reed arrow? Within a *li*, one bows before the scholar’s robes and cap. The immortal ascends into the void; emerging from the Hangu Pass, he preserves every stroke and dot. Within a single essay, several phrases encompass universal understanding;
within a single scroll, myriad words converge like rushing waters. Wind and clouds play between the gates of Changhe; the sun and moon rise beneath Mount Kunlun.

Liezi mounts them to ride through the heavens, while Zhoulai laughs at his observation of the correct. I have none— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The final sentence appears to be an incomplete thought or a rhetorical negation.)
I have attempted to fathom this book, yet I find myself unable to fathom it.
Written with humble prostrations by the fellow-disciple from Shanyin, Dharma-brother Qi Junjia (Dharma name Jingchao),
following twelve kinds of scriptures he has read and examined.
The Flower Ornament Verses, the Brahma Net Precepts, the Radiance of the Lankavatara Heart-Seal, the Eloquence of Vimalakirti,
the Pearl Necklace of Complete Enlightenment, the Questions and Answers of the Shurangama,
the Lamp Flame of Bhaisajyaguru, the Tongue-Phenomenon of Amitabha, and the Vajrasamadhi.
Verses on the Heart Sutra, the Introductory Discourse on the Lotus Sutra, the Final Verses of the Nirvana Sutra, and the Avatamsaka Sutra,
composed by the Chan monk Jingting, a successor in the Cao-Dong lineage.
Heojun (Heshun), Qiuyu Jushi Cao Rong,
Kuishi Daoren Zhu Maoshi, and Yue Shi read the "Chapter on the Sublime Adornment of the World."
Rowing a small boat at the head of Shili Beach, the white reeds and wild geese drift aimlessly. Where has the wooden boy ever been known?
With a single blast from the iron flute, return home and rest (Magadha).

I come to visit the village shop of Xiaoqiao during the spring season. Gently swaying, the cold plum blossoms burst open like spraying snow. Sitting for so long, I am unaware that my body is a traveler;
I linger back and forth between the mountain streams and the misty trees. (Maniyun)
The cuckoo cries out until the partridge calls; jade butterflies flutter about as the tree shadows blur.
There is no help for it at the place where flowers bloom by the front stream—a courtyard of flutes and pipes welcomes the yellow oriole. (In Praise of a Heavenly Deity)
Autumn mountains are desolate as the evening smoke settles; fallen leaves drift through the air, startling the birds at roost. For what reason do the scattered clouds move beyond the solitary peaks?
An old monk walks alone, carrying his gourd-bowl and straw hat. (Puxian)
The immortal gazes at the jade terrace through clouds; amidst the sound of the Yellow Bamboo, grief shakes the earth. Could it be that King Mu left his eight swift steeds here?
The misty waters of the Lesser Hill are near Penglai (the Sea of Flower-Treasury).
In the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Manifestation of Signs":
The heavens and seas are clear as clouds, a silver hare floats therein; Ten thousand miles of radiance flows through the Yangtze and Han rivers.
How much more so in this empty courtyard where white cranes soar, And the slanting shadows of emerald mountains fall upon crystal curtains.
In the Samādhi of Samantabhadra, a thousand fireflies flicker before a small window; their shadows upon half an acre of verdant moss gaze toward the heavens.
One cannot believe their radiance rivals that of the sun and moon—yet they are but decaying grass by the roadside for many years.
In the Chapter on the Accomplishment of the World:
A thousand peaks of icicle-flowers form jade towers; sea cranes fly as they return from the Fragrant Waters. In several places, pearl banners obscure the jeweled trees;
one suspects the Jade Isles have opened toward heaven.

In the world of Avataṃsaka, the peach-blossom grove blooms with overlapping reflections; atop Mount Huanghe, the misty scenery is thick and deep. To the left and right, the profusion of splendor is inexhaustible to behold;
the palaces of the azure pearls are sealed by colored clouds.
In the Chapter on Vairocana:
At Kongtong, he asked the Way—what was it he sought? The Imperial Son rode the dragon to roam upon the sea. To behold Guangcheng face-to-face is not far;
the shadows of azure clouds drift leisurely across the heavens.

From the "Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgata," a billion Mañjuśrīs cross shadows and arrive; mountain clouds and ocean trees grow ever more majestic. Do not mistake him for the old man riding the ox;
it is certain that the crystal peaks lie within Wutai.
In the Chapter on the Four Noble Truths, the lute is strummed and the spittoon struck; the huqin, flute, and pipes join in song and shout.
Where do these manifold sounds linger in their sorrowful resentment? They but sing the *zhègū* before the wind.
In the Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance, a single section of pearl curtains casts shimmering shadows; the light flies across the Milky Way as jade trees shift their form.
Men dwell within crystal palaces, where ice-clear vases reflect slantingly against azure lapis lazuli.
In the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Wisdom," the son of the Southern Land (Zhi Dun) lets forth a soaring song; Xu, Ruan, Ying, and Liu all fall into his net.
It is especially Zihuan (Cao Pi) who boasts of his clever artistry—playing *tanqi*, wielding the sword, and performing graceful dances.
In the "Chapter on Pure Conduct":

A thousand mu of fields under the blue banner welcome the spring sunshine; the sovereign himself hangs the plow and sets out with the dark-tipped ploughshare. How could he have allowed the imperial registers to remain idle in the cold wind?
He desires that all households learn the ways of farming.

From ancient times until now, the "True Man of the White Water" has appeared; he rose in the great wilds and brought the forests to peace. On the eastern frontier, he established the martial virtue that opened the royal enterprise;
his prudence and sincerity were the result of long-accumulated diligent effort.
Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru; in the midst of the "Verses Praising the Summit of Sumeru," I lean upon my companions and converse at ease.
White birds wheel and soar among the thousand-stemmed pines. Sitting upright and unmoving, I utterly forget whether it is morning or evening;
I suspect my body is actually atop the highest peak.

In the Hall of Broad Prospect, before the Gate of Yao’s Mother; at Zhaoyang Palace, the younger son sits upon the golden-rooted chariot. The precious cauldron of Xuanyuan is personally received and transmitted;
with ritual courtesy at Kunming, he serves the Most Honored One.
In the Chapter on the Brahma-Faring, a fragrant breeze sweeps through as the scent of lotus flowers wafts by. Upon a single pillow at the sand pavilion, one bids farewell to the setting sun.
Idly drifting a small boat for three or four li, the leaves of the lotuses flutter wildly, striking the mandarin ducks.
The Chapter on the Merit of First Resolving the Mind:
The towering Lion, most honored among beasts, who possesses three hundred hairs;
he alone permits Mañjuśrī as his companion, riding astride the blue-tailed one as he treads upon Mount Kunlun.

In the "Chapter on Clarifying the Dharma," the robes and caps of Confucius’ home village honor the court of Lu; for many years the Great Dipper has turned its course, and the *Lunyu* (Classic of the Analects) was composed. Magnificent seekers of the Way traveled from the capitals of Jing and Luo;
the Purple Qi of the Immortal Lord manifested his numinous power in half-measure.
Chapter on Ascending the Palace of Yama-deva; Chapter on Verses of Praise within the Palace of Yama-deva:
Rows of ethereal immortals stand in formation; amidst the sound of flutes and pipes, phoenixes dance. Their bodies are near the Gate of Changhe within the Qin palace;
a single melody from the Heavenly Court has long been familiar.
In the "Chapter on the Ten Practices," Liu Dezhiqu dared not shun toil; for many years he was so diligent that the hair on his calves fell away.
Though it is said in vain that he died as a traveler among the yellow bears, the numinous talisman of Shiniu remains high through the Feng and Shan sacrifices.
The Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries:
The void contains even a small gourd to its full extent. With a carefree, wild song, he fills the roads. It is not that this rustic man’s path is wicked;
he has long been a weathered veteran of the world.
Chapter on Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace; Chapter on Verses of Praise within the Tuṣita Palace:
The Unfailing (Weyang) Palace leans against the heavens as it opens; the radiance of Taiyi follows the night’s arrival. Who would have thought that the divine immortals practice songs and lyrics?
At the Baiyang Hall, the cycles of the year revolve with the talent of the planet Jupiter.
In the tenth stage of Dedication, the Five Elders once again journeyed by river; the dragon-horse need no longer boast of its many auspicious responses.
Within the thatched huts of the earthen steps, he felt pity for the common people, half of whom were afflicted by chronic illness.
The Ten Stages Realm is beautiful, with Lianong Mountain bordering Guangsang to the west. The azure seas are deep and profound, and the celestial path is lost to sight;
the Ten Continents lie far away and cannot be seen, while fragrances drift through the palace towers as colored clouds hang low.
In the Chapter on the Ten Samādhis:
Apricot blossoms drift down, willows like mist. All day long I sing wildly, falling into a drunken sleep.
The sound of the Qiang flute reaches ten thousand *li* within my dream, drifting chaotically with flying birds across the clear river.
Chapter Ten:
On Penetrating the Profound In a mountain deep, a humble cottage is the home of a man of the Way. The shadow of cranes falls upon the pine-clad stream; the stone steps slope away.
Ever since the Six Dynasties fell into chaos, Frost has chilled the clouds within his half-cave as he wears his aged *kāṣāya*.
Chapter Ten:

On the Ten Endurances The General gallops his steed across the Yin Mountains; Autumn grasses turn yellow, the crescent moon hangs low. His helmet is stained with blood, his beard and hair have turned white;
When will he return from outside the city of Shouxiang?
In the chapter on *asaṃkhyeya*, the tide turns a thousand times as it washes over the silver sands; the shimmering jade is vast and boundless, stretching far along the seashore.
Countless wild gulls fly on without ceasing, while white flowers to the east vomit forth the morning glow.
In the "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata," flowers bloom and fall year after year; neither studying Buddhism nor seeking immortality, one preserves the leisurely cycle of years at Wuling,
wandering freely as roosters and dogs follow their own destiny.

The dwelling places of the various Bodhisattvas follow one another like ravines ascending to the celestial terrace. Gathering medicinal herbs, he departed in his prime and has not returned. In the silent reaches of the rivers and plains, where can one inquire?
The stone bridge still awaits the arrival of the old man.

In the "Chapter on the Buddha’s Inconceivable Dharma," one gazes from afar at the capital city from Mount Xuanyu; it is empty. The Seven Sages wander in confusion, their minds still harboring attachments.
They vainly seek the Mysterious Pearl to summon the *wangxiang*, yet by riding the wind for a single night, they arrive in Huaxu.
In the "Chapter on the Ocean of the Tathāgata’s Ten Bodies," one bowl traverses ten thousand mountains at will.
Amidst drifting white clouds, the shadow lingers on and off. I pity my own emaciated bones heaped among the wild grass;
who recognizes this old bhikṣu from the Western Heaven?

In the "Chapter on the Merit of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks and Radiance," the palace halls of Sweet Spring (Ganquan) gathered a thousand officials. Emperor Wu personally bestowed the Dew-Receiving Basin;
it was most excellent that its golden stem encased the precious moon, its shadow a perfect orb upon the palm of the immortal.
In the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Conduct," the morning brings various performances that dot the light clouds. Spitting fire and swallowing swords are deeds beyond the common;
upon the plains, fish and dragons spread out in succession, while the wealthy guests of the Five Tombs watch them in their profusion.
In the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," dewdrops fall from the ponds after the rain has passed. On both banks, lotuses are covered with green duckweed.
From the tall trees, the birds' songs resound repeatedly; a swarm of butterflies dances among the dragonflies.

The Sword Arts Tradition of the *Lishijian-pin* (Chapter on Leaving the World) originated from Bai Xuan. His yellow-robed dancing sleeves alone soar aloft. Mount Kunlun turns to the left, leaning upon the Southern Pole;
the stars of Taiyi are arrayed, and the Celestial Market is level and vast.

The pearl curtains are stirred by a gentle breeze, their shadows layering one another; three thousand women with powdered faces and dark brows appear lush with moisture. Together they ascend to invite the Immortal and pay homage to the Queen Mother;
scattered coral and jade lotuses lie in disarray.
To the south of Mount Jiuyi, half the inhabitants are jackals and wolves; the severed-haired Jiaoxiao weep in the Great Wilderness.
Even if one were to swallow two suns and not die, how could it cause the barbarian courts to recognize the King?
Azure cranes and dragon-boats amidst the sound of flutes and drums; Flowers fall in the rear courtyard as the wind fills the river. A single strain from the *konghou* lute sends people into a dream;
The slanting sun before the eastern mountains draws a rainbow across the sky.
Shouldering his staff, he wanders to the ends of the earth; smoke from broken tombs mists the traveler’s slanting path. At night, amidst the frost, he tramples the moon beyond the clouds;
across the stream, two or three thatched cottages stand.

Crowned and girdled, he ascends through the heavens from Jianzhang Palace; Lapis lazuli fans and the fragrance of the imperial incense burner fill the air. Last night at the Fengshan sacrifice, the fungus-canopy lingered;
As an attendant, I personally received the radiance of the white jade.
Vaguely, the four eyes recognize Fangxiang; at midnight, headless, they run wild and frantic. It is precisely the King of Ghosts who can initiate his hegemony;
the purple-clad attendants joyfully form rows like the hubs of chariots.
White wolves and white deer fill the mountain peaks; King Mu travels far and wide toward the north. On his return journey, Lord Tang is intoxicated by the wine of the immortals;
furthermore, divine birds dance upon Mount Kunlun.
A million devas and humans, bearing jeweled swords, personally followed the phoenix carriage as it trod through the clouds and mists.
Relying on their feathered canopies to transmit military orders, they achieved great merit in subduing demons and malevolent spirits.
The Kukkutapāda Stūpa opens toward the horizon; golden bells and precious chimes are set upon its lofty tiers.
Its circular shadows fall for three thousand *zhang*, as Aśoka arrives simultaneously with his prophecy.
*Entering the Dharma Realm Chapter*:
Last night, celestial immortals descended upon the small pavilion; ice peaches and jade lotuses drifted through the air.

Amidst the distant mountains where phoenixes and cranes cried out, they spoke of this human world as the continent of Kukūṭapāda. (Mañjuśrī manifested the Lion-Stretching Samādhi; extending his hand, he touched [the master’s] crown, and suddenly vanished.)
The Daoist Xu Xuan comes from across the sea; he wanders aimlessly through the Han capital’s towers and gates. Night after night, the sound of the waves reaches the land of Fusan;
though there are a thousand doors of cypress and willow, he departs and does not return. (The Tower of Mañjuśrī, the Tower of Maitreya)
Golden flowers fly in abundance throughout the Huālín Garden; cloud-borne canopies of *zhī* fungi support the sun as it shines in full warmth.
The celestial palace of Paranirmita-vaśavartin is not far at all—let us follow the example of the Śāla grove in Jeta’s Forest and dare not forget our words.
At the tavern on the roadside ten *li* away, the innkeeper is busy as travelers ask for directions. How pitiable, hearts breaking amidst the sound of the flute;
a cluster of fishermen’s songs accompanies the setting sun (the journey of Sudhana’s southern quest).
Gazing afar, the mountain fields and landscapes stretch on and on; Residual snow fills my head as bamboo branches droop low. Frosty clouds pierce through the path of the cold crags;
There, another Hu monk crosses the waters to the west (De-un meets him).
By the White Heron Pond, autumn grasses abound; I ask how it fares at the Bamboo Grove Vihāra. The Buddha-lamps of a thousand homes awaken lingering dreams;
here, the sound of bells fills the songs of the oars (bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī).
I have heard it said that the Celestial Consort skillfully wields her shuttle; when the palace quarters are hushed, she begs for the golden waves.
Now, melons and fruits are offered year after year—who can cross the river with the Oxherd’s shadow? (The Upāsikā)
Strolling leisurely on horseback toward Chang’an, the people of Xinfeng fill my sight, none yet destroyed.
How much more so this night of lanterns in the six thoroughfares—drunk, I lean my slanted sable hat against the balustrade. (The Elder; the Householder; the Youth Male; the Youth Female)
The eccentric scholars of Yan and Qi flaunted their refined elegance; Huo Guang personally enfeoffed Wu Li as a Marquis. Hearing of the Way in Chengdu, he relied on chicken divination;
the man from Shu, Yang Yi, was most devoted [to him]. (Vimukha Rishi)

Lightning strikes and thunder roars as radiance flashes across the heavens; the shadows of dragons and *chī* stir as one beholds flying immortals. In an instant, the azure void and the vast sky grow still;
the crescent moon and stars hang suspended, linked with the Milky Way (*Śreṣṭha-brahmaṇa*, the Most Tranquil Brahmin).
The horned children joyfully gather sand; Without cause, the shadow of their stupa spreads across the world. They gaze upon each other as cowherds blow long flutes;
Wild geese returning to the river carry the setting glow of the sunset. (The River Islet Child is skilled in all arts; the Child of the Horned Youth.)
The hero’s hands are stained with blood; sword and blade are deployed with a single-minded resolve.
If one can conquer the enemy through refined song alone, let him sit upright in a silk turban and play the lute (King Anabhibhū of the City of Wonderful Light).
Having traversed the void, he trampled the minor celestial māras; taking each other by the hand, they crossed over Vulture Peak. Alone, he rows his boat and gazes out upon the river;
the sandy islets stretch far away, covered in lush green sedge. (The Universalist Heretic, Upatiṣya, and the Boatman).
A single song by Zhaojun is most soul-stirring; the lute on horseback brushes away traces of tears.

There is further resentment over the "crow-yellow" [hair dye] and youth gone by, as she suddenly leans upon her silver flute to compose the "Changmen" [Palace] poem (referring to the women Pāśupatī and Gopā).
The martial energy of Chiyou stirred the celestial patterns; the banners of the Han generals were heard throughout the world. The blade-drum was fully prepared, yet its course remained unknown;
the lingering valor of General Li remains at Lantian—Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Samantagāmin Bodhisattva.
With half his Sumeru body, he trampled upon the celestial palaces; dancing with his staff, he cast it back into a mustard seed. Most grievous was the Asura who obstructed the sun and moon;
let us cease speaking further of Zhuanche and Fengfang (the Great Deity).
Ten *li* before the mountain lies the shrine of the Great King; there drums are beaten and the *Bi* hymns are blown as the seasons pass. Only let every person cherish plowing and digging;
Pingyang is but a few inches from the realm of Yiqi (the Lord of the Earth and the Lord of the Forest).
Great horns hang down from the Milky Way to the east; the *zhiji* stone floats near the palaces of the Dipper and Ox. Far away, the moon’s essence casts lingering shadows;
I crane my neck toward its radiant glory throughout the night (O Lord of Night).
Following one another from Mount Tiangemu, we enjoy our delight; emerald grasses reach to the sky, holding jade flasks.
Turning my head toward the small hills beyond the jade trees, white phoenixes dance upon the wind as they greet Lady Magu (the celestial maiden, Lady Māyā).
The Wayfarer of Changting sleeps with his head in his arms; the multi-storied pavilions lean askew as he drags his cloth bag.
With a snap of the fingers he knows there is nothing else—originally, he was merely seeking a single coin (Maitreya).
A single thread of golden brocade passed down from Kāśyapa; mountains, rivers, and the great earth dance with fluttering grace.
It was personally acquired within the practice of *dhūta*; it does not reside in the triviality of a mere smile (Puxian).
The Universal Worthy’s Vows and Practices:
A full-bodied water buffalo in an open field; beneath the green willows and fragrant grasses, all is tranquil and vast. For years the crops have relied upon its strength;
with hooves and horns facing the wind, it moves entirely at its own ease.
*Avataṃsaka Sūtra Verses* (End).
Preface to *The Radiance of the Brahma Net Precepts* by Master Lingting.

Whenever I see those who carry a single board [who hold one-sided views], as soon as they step through the gateway, they immediately intend to negate cause and effect. As for those who believe, accept, and practice [the teachings]:
Furthermore, many more piles are being driven and the rafters are being struck. How bitter!

I pray that the Venerable Master will give rise to great compassion, manifest the mark of the broad and long tongue, and provide intimate instruction on the heart-essence of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Crush it into a single lump and cause all sentient beings throughout the great earth to realize it directly;

only then will you know that when the Old Barbarian faced the wall, he had already placed the entire *Brahmajāla Sūtra* upon the platter before you. Should you hesitate for even a moment, the light of the precepts will vanish ten thousand miles away.
Postscript by the Daoist Shibo of Yue’an:
The Radiance of the Brahmajāla Sūtra Precepts,
composed by the Bhikṣu Jingting of the ancient Zisheng Monastery.
Read by the fellow students of Yuyan: Yang Yongjian, Jing Song,
Xu Xuling, and Jing Yue, [upon reading] the Upper and Lower Sections of the "Bodhisattva’s Chapter on the Ground of the Mind."
"How is it that great practitioners wear fur and carry horns? How is it that great practitioners kill people and set fires?
Do you all understand this? If you do understand, then every step you take is none other than the site of enlightenment (dōjō).
Whether acting contrarily or in accord with the flow, your entire being is fully utilized; the Prātimokṣa has been expounded in its entirety at once."
The light of the precepts issues from the mouth; it is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white. The Buddhas of the three periods speak the precepts simultaneously with one voice.
Can all people still hear them? In the age of the final dharma, bhikṣus treat the precepts with contempt;
they regard the *poṣadha* held every half-month as a mere formal document. There are those among the followers of "mad wisdom" who neglect dignified decorum and do not restrain their conduct.

I examine this and say: the "Moving and Leading Spring Great Way," "Drunken Bag," "Chang'an Wine Immortal," and "Clam Monk"—this entire band of perverse practitioners—has fashioned themselves into a protective talisman, claiming that it is the insight that is valued, not the practice.
But how could the rites have been established for people such as these? Alas, alas! King Yama has prepared for them the mountain of knives, the forest of swords, and the cauldron of molten copper.
"I have been waiting for you for a long time on this iron bed. When the light of the eyes falls to the ground, this mouth of yours will be of no further use.
The precepts are like the sun and moon, and like a necklace of pearls; since the time of the Seven Buddhas, they have been upheld as the ritual code.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, the Sūtra of Precepts was called the "Ambrosial Drum. During the time of Kanakamuni Buddha...
The Prātimokṣa Sūtra is called the "Mirror of the Dharma. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, the Prātimokṣa Sūtra was called the "Discernment of Emptiness.
Now, under Śākyamuni Buddha, the Prātimokṣa Sūtra is called the "Brahmajāla" (Brahma’s Net). Great Brahmā Devendra established a great net-like banner, with light interpenetrating light.
The world is like the mesh of a net; the Dharma-gates are likewise like the mesh of a net. Have any of you ever seen them? The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* has sixty-one chapters;
this "Mind-Ground" chapter is the tenth. How extraordinary! How extraordinary! The "Yellow-Faced Old Man" is the Reward Body Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*).
The original source, Vairocana, is the Dharma Body Buddha (*dharmakāya*). And the billions of Śākyamunis—
This is the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha. You emit light, and I also emit light; they mingle as one mass and blend into a single whole.
One knows not who is host and who is guest, who is bright and who is dark. Light enters light like the banners of Indra’s net—truly a magnificent spectacle to behold.
Yet I must ask you: can this be the light of the precepts? This cannot be the light of the precepts.
"Ma! If you say it is this very thing, Śākyamuni Buddha clearly stated that it is not blue, yellow, red, or white.
If you say it is something apart from this, then what exactly is it within this palace of purple-gold vajra radiance?
It cannot be affirmed, nor can it be denied; it cannot be grasped, nor can it be relinquished. Try and offer me a single phrase. Is it so? It is so."
The Dharmakāya has two kinds of illnesses and two kinds of lights; the ancients have already made this perfectly clear.
Yet these dozing fellows chase after mere fragments like this—what end will there ever be? Śākyamuni was an adept at putting on airs;
he willingly hid his body among slaves and servants, then pushed out that one Honored One, the Original Vairocana Buddha, to point east and speak.
West. Take three, five. As for this Vairocana Buddha—whether his surname be Zhang or Li, let us not concern ourselves with that—he is ultimately the Crown Prince of King Śuddhodana.
He has come here accompanied by them as companions, like a shadow following a form.
These thousands of millions of minor Śākyamunis are likewise the manifestations of his own spirit, a class of solitary ghosts who have taken refuge in grass and wood to shift their forms.
That which is transformed is not me; I am precisely that. It is like a household ghost playing with its own family members: the speaker speaks and the listener listens, making a fine spectacle.
At that time, had the Heavenly King Maheśvara known how to employ a bit of skillful maneuvering, he would have simply closed the main gate and forbidden him from entering.
Let us see what kind of face the Yellow-Faced Gautama would have had then!
What more need be said of the "ten-thousand-foot Dharma-body" and the "hundred-billion transformation-bodies"? It is commonly said that the Dharma-body is formless;
yet here, upon this majestic lotus throne, one speaks of the Buddha-dharma with such earnestness and persistence. Furthermore, it is called the "original source Dharma-body.
But as soon as one reaches the vicinity of the Dharma-body, there is still no phrase that penetrates the Dharma-body. Do you know Xiantong?
After a year, one might speak of that which is above the Dharma-body. Last night, the rain fell in torrents, knocking down the grape arbor.
The administrators mobilized the assembly; some propped it up, others supported it. Propping and supporting, propping and supporting, until daybreak—it remains as pitiable as ever.
What difference is there between this and the ox of Huai-chou or the horse of Yi-chou? Let us set aside these entanglements for now.
Cease. The ten minds of departure, the ten minds of nurturing, the ten adamantine minds, and the ten stages—these are called the "Minds of the Ground" (*cittabhūmi*).
What are the mind of departure, the mind of nurturing, and the adamantine mind? On the road to Mount Tai, I have burned away my commentaries and sub-commentaries.
Whether past, present, or future, the mind cannot be found when sought. Is it the physical heart-mass, the discursive mind of conceptualization, or the *tathatā*-mind?
Cast the mind of nirvana all at once toward other worlds—beyond that, and beyond that. What is there to say about becoming a Buddha from the source within the thirty minds?
What of the ten stages (*bhūmi*)? These five directions and five lands are called the ten stages.
What need is there to speak of the first stage, the second, the third, fourth, or fifth, up to the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages? And what of the mind of relinquishment?
In the pond, yellow birds play with dragonflies; how can one cultivate the mind of precept-keeping? The earth god does not eat meat; how can one cultivate the mind of forbearance?
The wind turns the corner of the hall and the dog shakes its bell; how can one cultivate the mind of diligence? Help me devise a single ingot of gold.
How is the mind of concentration? Three inches of eyebrows press down upon the eyes. How is the mind of wisdom? You head toward Xiangxiang; I head toward Qin. How is the mind of protection?
A single scroll of the *Lingfu Zhouhou Jing* (Scripture of the Spirit Talisman for the Back of the Elbow). How is the mind of joy? Every house has its bright moon;
the stars fill the heavens. How is the mind of the crown? Three pounds of iron behind the skull of Mount Kunlun. How is the mind of compassion? A cat.
A child catching a mouse with feigned innocence—what is the mind of compassion? An old white-forehead tiger on the Southern Mountain who has become a spirit—what is the mind of joy?
A bald-headed youth sounding a wind-fiddle—what is the mind of equanimity? A centenarian dividing his night-lamp—what is the mind of giving?
Half a liang of yellow hellebore plus fine asarum—what is the mind of kind speech? A forced smile of welcome—[what is the mind of benefit]?
How to give rise to the mind of anger? Prince Bodhi explains it clearly. How to unify the mind? A pair of mandarin ducks embroidered with exquisite care.
How to settle the mind? A boatman rowing at the edge of the great river. How to cultivate the mind of wisdom? The scenery of Hao and Pu remains fresh after a thousand years.
How to cultivate the mind of faith? A crimson rooster and a white dog form a fine friendship. How to cultivate the mind of mindfulness?
The mind: having lost the calf-toe cloth worn at the hearth, how can one turn it toward enlightenment? The Vajra does not consent to being split into pieces; how can one penetrate the mind?
The rhinoceros develops patterns on its horn from gazing at the moon; how can one maintain a straightforward mind? When the basin strikes the jar, the jar strikes the basin;
how can one maintain a non-regressing mind? The general’s iron horse gallops double the distance; how can one maintain the Mahayana mind? The windlass...
A pulley and rope weigh a thousand *qun*; how is this the mind of signlessness (*animitta*)? A single hook and three dots are too much confusion;

how is this the mind of wisdom (*prajñā*)? When the comet appears, the people fall ill; how is this the indestructible mind (*akṣaya-citta*)? Lighting a funeral pyre for a deceased monk wastes firewood;
how is this the level ground (*samatā-bhūmi*)? You, *ācārya*, see only the sharp point of the awl; how is this the ground of skillful wisdom (*kalyāṇa-prajñā-bhūmi*)? On the boat—
The old fisherman does not have the surname Xie; how can this be the Ground of Radiance? The sounds of songs and flutes from the pavilions are faint and delicate;
how can this be the Ground of Blazing Flames? You have mistaken the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West; how can this be the Ground of Skillful Illumination?
Three monkeys try to guess a riddle in silence; how can this be the Ground of Flowering Light? The golden crow shines in the day and at midnight; how can this be the Ground of Fulfillment? Chang’an.
The Great Way is a long play. How is it on the ground of the Buddha’s roar? Clapping hands while speaking of the ultimate truth at a lantern. How is it on the ground of the Avataṃsaka?
Striking one's head and bumping one's forehead, there is no way to avoid it. How is it on the ground of the Buddha-realm?

When hungry, one eats; when weary, one sleeps. Truly laughable, truly laughable! This single scroll of the Brahmajāla Sūtra is so convoluted and jagged that one cannot even read it by sentence or clause. All quarters [of the Buddhist world]...
Students habitually attempt to force their understanding by fitting these words and phrases together; this is already a mistake.
Now, I shall explain the sutra through the sutra itself, and cannot help but once again expound upon the very words of the original scripture as an offering to the assembly.

What is relinquishment (*tyāga*)? It is the relinquishing of all that is internal and the relinquishing of all that is external; the relinquishing of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the relinquishing of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
There is nothing—not even the single unified characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) of the aggregates, bases, and elements—that is not relinquished. This is called relinquishment. What is precept (*śīla*)?
It is neither precept nor non-precept. It has no recipient and no accumulator; it is the departure from all natures (*sarvadharmavigata*). This is called precept. What is patience (*kṣānti*)?

The patience of emptiness, the patience of all places, the patience of non-arising, the patience of suffering, the patience of immeasurable practices, and even the patience regarding the self, persons, bondage, liberation, and the suchness of all phenomena—since the characteristics of patience cannot be apprehended, this is called patience. What is diligence?
It is ascending the mountain of non-arising; whether existent or non-existent, there is neither entering nor non-entering—this is called diligence. What is concentration? Not...

Quiescent and extinguished; moment by moment, quiescent and extinguished—this is called concentration (*samādhi*). What is wisdom (*prajñā*)? It is neither fruit nor cause; neither ordinary nor noble; neither sin nor merit;
neither bondage nor liberation; it is not the eight inversions. Without arising or ceasing, it knows through non-conditioning—this is called wisdom. What is the vow (*praṇidhāna*)?
It is the aspiration-mind following upon the aspiration-mind, continuing in succession without interruption. This is...
The essential nature of aspiration can ultimately not be apprehended; this is called aspiration. What is protection?
That all persons and non-arising phenomena are clearly illuminated by light—that is protection. Even that which arises through illusion is as non-existent as non-existence;
this is called protection. What is joy? Not entering into the conditioned, yet not being devoid of tranquility—this is called joy. What is the crown? As...

The Peak Contemplation (*mūrdhan*) is continuous. This continuity is like the peak itself; one perceives neither conditions nor non-conditions. This is called the Peak. What is loving-kindness (*maitrī*)?
It is without arising, abiding, or ceasing, being like an illusion or a transformation. This is called loving-kindness. What is compassion (*karuṇā*)?
It is the equalization of friend and enemy, self and other, in a single bliss. This is called compassion. What is sympathetic joy (*muditā*)? It is the departure from all existence. This is called...
What is joy? It is the equal and singular illumination; this is called joy. What is equanimity? It is neither joining nor dispersing; this is called equanimity. What is generosity?
It is acting in accordance with the Buddha’s intent; this is called generosity. What is beneficial speech?
It is entering the Samādhi of Benefit and shaking the world, even manifesting forms within the six realms of existence to [relieve] immeasurable suffering.
To not regard affliction as a calamity is called "benefit. How is this "sameness"? To divide the body and disperse the form through the wisdom of non-self is called "sameness.
How is this "concentration"? To be without arising and without activity is called "concentration. How is this "wisdom"?
Radiant brilliance and penetrating clarity such that there is no recipient [of sensation] is called "wisdom. How is this "faith"? Because the mind is empty.
To believe that the person and the name are ultimately unattainable—this is called faith (*śraddhā*). What is mindfulness (*smṛti*)?

Transformation, transmutation, abiding together, and simultaneous occurrence—this is called mindfulness. What is the profound mind (*gambhīracitta*)? To enter deeply into emptiness and to attain profound liberation—this is the profound mind.
What is penetration (*prativedha*)? To thoroughly penetrate the emptiness of all phenomena—this is called penetration.
"Attainment. What is 'direct' (*ṛju*)? To be without fetters and without bondage—this is called direct. What is 'non-retrogression'?

Not abiding in retrogression, not acting in retrogression, and not thinking in retrogression; being singularly pure and singularly illuminating—this is non-retrogression. What is the 'Great Vehicle' (*mahāyāna*)?

The vehicle of wisdom and the vehicle of practice, which carry and employ all—this is the Great Vehicle. What is 'signlessness' (*animitta*)? Not departing from deluded thoughts while explaining and liberating."
Liberated illumination. To teach the dharmas of the three periods of time without severing the bonds of karma—this is called signlessness (*animitta*).

What is wisdom (*prajñā*)? To enter into all dharmas without accumulation and without grasping—this is called wisdom. What is indestructibility (*akṣaya*)? Entering the realm of Māra without being destroyed;
entering the sovereignty of the Buddha—this is called indestructibility. What is equanimity (*samatā*)? Entering immeasurable buddha-fields from a single buddha-field; [entering] a single eon...
Entering immeasurable kalpas, one takes that which is inexpressible and makes it expressible. Reflecting back upon both the contrary and the compliant, all are seen as dharmas.

Constantly entering the two truths while abiding within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one knows the twelve links of dependent origination and the nature of the ten evils, yet remains eternally established in the wholesome paths.
Entering the ten branches of dhyāna and practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one manifests as non-path. This is called "Equanimity" (*sama*).

...and so forth. What is skillful wisdom (*suvijñāna*)? It is that which, relying on the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, abandons all attachment, practices universal equanimity, and contemplates the limit of emptiness (*śūnyatā-koṭi*) of all phenomena.
One regards earth, water, fire, and wind as all having been one's own former bodies, and contemplates bestowing equal happiness upon all sentient beings to be transformed;
this is skillful wisdom. What is radiance (*prabhā*)? It is the practice of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in this manner.
I have long since been free from marks (*lakṣaṇa*). I enter into the light of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), dhāraṇīs, and eloquence (*pratibhāna*), traveling through buddha-fields.

Within a single sound, I preach immeasurable categories of Dharma; this is what constitutes "light. How could there be such "flames"? Such flames are both conventional and ultimate, neither interrupted nor permanent, neither one nor two.
Abiding in the ten kinds of awakening, I enter deeply into the fruits of meditative concentration and employ skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to transform and teach beings.

Sentient beings—this is your radiance. How does wisdom illuminate? Being fully endowed with the ten powers, one knows the causes and effects of one's own cultivation, and likewise knows the causes and effects of all sentient beings.
One transforms pure lands into evil lands, and evil lands into lands of wondrous bliss.
One turns good into evil, and evil into good. One turns form into non-form, and non-form into form. One takes a man as...
To regard a woman as a man, the six realms of existence as not being the six realms, and that which is not the six realms as the six realms—this is the illumination of wisdom (*prajñā*). How so?
The Light of the Flower (*Puṣpārāma*) causes wondrous flowers to bloom and emits various kinds of light; the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) are fully perfected, manifesting immeasurable bodies.
The distinct functions of mind and speech are inexhaustible—this is the Light of the Flower. How so? It is because it fulfills all dharmas.
He constantly dwells in the samādhi of the Middle Way, fully endowed with the six categories.
Abiding in this, it is a dharma not shared with those of the lower stages, even among the eighteen mental samādhis of the noble ones. All sentient beings are my parents;
all dharmas practiced by all Buddhas, including all dharma-gates from the eighth to the ninth stage, I have already entered and fully perfected. How could the Buddha...?

Hūṃ! Entering the Samādhi of the Dharma-King’s Throne, one possesses the ten grades of the Great Illumination Gate of Emptiness, unspeakably unspeakable supernormal powers and wisdom, hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates, hundreds of thousands of samādhi gates, and hundreds of thousands of Vajra gates.

The hundreds of thousands of gates of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the hundreds of thousands of gates of liberation (*vimokṣa*) are all fully possessed in a single thought-moment and at a single time.

This extends even to the illumination of returning, the illumination of following, and the illumination of reversing; the illumination of the preceding and the illumination of the succeeding; the illumination of cause and the illumination of fruit; the illumination of emptiness and the illumination of existence;
and the illumination of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way. This is the Lion’s Roar of the Buddha. How is this so? In the *Avataṃsaka*, there is no coming or going in the Tathāgata’s samādhi.
At that time, within the three thousandfold world system, he manifested Buddha-activities: turning the realm of Māra into the realm of the Buddha, and the realm of the Buddha into the realm of Māra;

turning all views into the view of the Buddha, and the view of the Buddha into all views; the Buddha-nature entering the nature of sentient beings, and the nature of sentient beings entering the Buddha-nature.
Blazing with radiant flames, there was a single path of purity. All sentient beings are my father.
O Mother! To the non-Buddhists and the celestial Māras, you appear as their own parents.

Abiding in this stage, from the limit of birth-and-death to the limit of the diamond-like samādhi, you transform immeasurable realms within a single thought-moment; this is the Avataṃsaka. How so? Within the Buddha-realm, emptiness is further emptied, and emptiness is again emptied.
Entering the nature of empty space, one perceives the wisdom of equality. Thus is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, World-Knower, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One—this "Buddha-ground" is the locus entered by all noble beings among these ten titles; this is the Buddha-realm. Such is the mind.

Such grounds, such chapters and phrases, such words—having been spoken and fully spoken, having been annotated and fully annotated—the ancient, thousand-year-old wit Vairocana Buddha speaks for himself and listens for himself. He deceives the dull-witted and ignorant;

thus he strikes the drum to close the gate of the profound mystery (*paramārtha*). The sound of the drum is outside; one must know that there is a matter for all to recognize, yet none at all understand it.
I have deceived you. Do you see? Do you see? There, beneath the Bodhi tree, he sits upon his seat just as it was. Yet, in an instant, he is preaching the Dharma in the Hall of Sublime Light;

in an instant, he is preaching the Dharma in the palace of Śakra; in an instant, he is preaching the Dharma among the Yāma devas; in an instant, he is preaching the Dharma among the Cāturmahārājika devas;
in an instant, he is preaching the Dharma in the Nirmāṇarati heaven; in an instant, he is [preaching the Dharma] in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven.

Nourishment is consciousness; non-nourishment is wisdom. Obstruction is consciousness; non-obstruction is wisdom. Conjunction and correspondence are consciousness.
Non-obstruction is wisdom (*jñāna*); grasping at characteristics is consciousness (*vijñāna*). Not grasping at characteristics is wisdom; gathering [objects] is consciousness;
not gathering is wisdom. Are there two kinds? People are turned by the twelve hours of the day, but this old monk can turn the twelve hours.
This is not a wild fox spirit transforming itself in such a way. It is the transformation of form, the transformation of characteristics, and the turning of causes.

Transformation: transformation of form, transformation of perception, transformation of nature, transformation of the clarity of conditions, transformation of the clarity of actions, and transformation of phenomena.
Of which non-Buddhist school do you belong? The continuity of the five destinies has no end;
it is a continuity of attachment to signs, a continuity of attachment to conditions, and a continuity of attachment to existence and non-existence, arising from the delusion of birth and non-birth.

The continuity of conceptual attachment to signs; the continuity of conceptual attachment to the extinction or non-extinction [of phenomena]; the continuity of conceptual attachment to vehicles and non-vehicles;
the continuity of conceptual attachment to the conditioned and the unconditioned; the continuity of conceptual attachment to the specific characteristics of each stage (*bhūmi*);

the continuity of conceptual attachment to one's own discursive thoughts and uninterrupted delusions; and the reliance on the dualistic categories of existence and non-existence by those of external paths.
The continuity of conceptual attachment to marks; the uninterrupted continuity of conceptual attachment to the three vehicles and the one vehicle. Now, I must ask you:
before a single thought arises, is there a severance of the anterior and posterior limits, or does it continue? That which is able to continue is called the "Lord of Lords.
This is the meaning of continuity; this is the meaning of liberation. The noble wisdom perceives the nature; the ignorant and foolish do not perceive the nature.
Noble wisdom is without self-nature. It is only in response to the delusions of ordinary people that noble wisdom is said to have a nature.

The Buddhas of the three periods do not know that it exists; the black oxen and white cows, however, know that it exists. Knowing that it exists, they yet do not know that it exists; by not knowing that it exists, they achieve the knowledge that it exists.
All phenomena are unborn; one should not establish a thesis regarding them. A wooden man walking, a barren woman conceiving—these are the meaning of birth, these are the meaning of non-birth.
It is birth that is non-birth; it is not that there is no birth and thus one speaks of non-birth. It is knowing that is non-knowing.
It is not that one speaks of "ignorance" while being ignorant. To discern a preceding object is not what is called "knowledge.

That which is "knowledge" is that which has nothing to be known in any place whatsoever. Why? Because there is neither ignorance nor non-ignorance. Why? Because it cannot be known by means of cognition.

Is it that first there is function and subsequently illumination? Or first illumination and subsequently function? Are illumination and function simultaneous? Or are illumination and function distinct?

At that time, there are four permutations: removing the person but not the object; removing the object but not the person; removing both the person and the object; and removing neither the person nor the object. These are all skillful means.
Those who are ordinary and ignorant lack wisdom; they become attached to these provisional teachings and fail to discern them properly.
How can one deal with the four propositions of our own school?

Whether it be worldly discourse, the treatises of non-Buddhists (*ābhidharma*), miscellaneous discussions, street talk, local dialects, songs, or even sneezing, spitting, yawning, and sighing—there is nothing that is not the Buddha-work. Nevertheless, nevertheless, worldly speech is manifold and unreal;
it increases discursive entangment (*ālambana*) and becomes mere deluded thought (*vikalpa*). This remains so even down to the slightest state of mind.
Consciousness flows and falsely discriminates external objects; this is the thief that has been apprehended. It is neither existent nor empty, neither expressible nor inexpressible.
The ninety-six circular signs represent the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika).
They are neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa, yet those non-Buddhists each cling to a single sign—some taking the extinction of fire to be nirvāṇa, others taking the stilling of wind to be nirvāṇa.
...or they take nirvāṇa to be the destruction of the perceiver and the perceived; or they take nirvāṇa to be the view of permanence and impermanence;
or they take nirvāṇa to be the view of signlessness; or they take nirvāṇa to be the indestructibility of an intrinsic nature;
or they take nirvāṇa to be the destruction of all phenomena; or they take nirvāṇa to be the transformation of the guṇas; or...
That is to say, some claim it is the exhaustion of merit and demerit; others claim it is the exhaustion of all afflictions (*kleśa*); others take wisdom to be *nirvāṇa*.
Some perceive the sovereign lack of agency in sentient beings and their false conceptualizations as *nirvāṇa*.

Others hold that the cycle of birth and death among sentient beings proceeds without any further cause, and through such clinging they conceive of it as *nirvāṇa*. Or they say they have attained the Truth.
Some regard the Truths and the Path as themselves Nirvāṇa. Some perceive Nirvāṇa through the union, identity, difference, or both-and-not-both of these.

Some reckon that all things arise from spontaneity (*svabhāva*) and thus cling to spontaneity itself as Nirvāṇa. Some claim that one attains Nirvāṇa by understanding the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*).
Some seek Nirvāṇa by protecting the state and adhering to the *Ṣaḍguṇya-vinaya* (the treatise on the six virtues). Or...
They perceive the seasons and the world as nirvana; some call it "nature," others call it "non-nature";
some claim that by knowing nature and non-nature one achieves nirvana; or they see a distinction between awakening and nirvana and thereby achieve nirvana.
In such various ways, the non-Buddhists each cling to their own single path, unable to reach a definitive resolution at the shore of birth and death. Do you understand?
Do you understand? That which is nirvāṇa is without birth and without cessation; it is without object and without cause; it is free from grasping and transcends all falsehood;
it is neither permanent nor impermanent; it is neither an agent nor an action; it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; it is neither the subject of awakening nor the object of awakening;

it is neither a characteristic nor that which is characterized; it is neither the aggregates nor distinct from the aggregates; it is neither speech nor that which is spoken; it is neither one nor different.
It is neither simultaneous nor non-simultaneous. One should know that "neither arising nor ceasing" is another name for the Tathāgata.
Within the Sahā world, the Tathāgata has three hundred thousand asaṃkhyeya names; like the moon in water, he neither comes forth nor enters.
The Tathāgata is not non-manifest within this; all the words and expressions of the sūtras speak fluently of neither-arising-nor-ceasing, yet these words have no real meaning whatsoever.
Why? Because the nature of letters is devoid [of intrinsic reality].
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not speak a single word, nor do they answer a single word. For forty-nine years, not a single word was spoken. Take this as...
Is it not that you were close to the Buddha and yet misheard him? This old monk’s staff is quite lively!

If one thoroughly understands all dharmas, all stages, and all characteristics, and masters the words and phrases while being fully endowed with their essential meaning, then one can take the joy of formlessness as one's own recreation, establish sentient beings in the equal Mahāyāna, and embrace them in the Right Dharma.
When the lineage of the Dharma-Buddha is not severed, one is able to understand the sublime points of entry and constantly attains transformation-birth (*upapāduka*).

Through the ten powers of mastery, one manifests various forms and preaches the Dharma according to reality. Do you understand? Do you understand? A prince born by transformation treads upon the crown of Vairocana’s head;
his emanated bodies spread transformation throughout the lands of the ten directions. Therefore, this is not a matter of external succession, nor is it that of a subject.
Do you understand? Do you understand? The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is beyond verbal expression and pointers.
As for those non-Buddhists who speak of the unarisen and undying—[namely] first, time; second, space; third, emptiness; fourth, atoms; fifth, the four great elements;
sixth, Mahābrahmā; seventh, Śakra; eighth, Maheśvara; ninth, Īśvara, the Lord of Beings—is this [the truth]? No, no, no! This is birth.
Is this non-arising? Is it cessation? Or is it non-cessation? Within the twelve links of dependent origination, there is no hooking or locking internally or externally;

craving and attachment are clearly revealed as being composed of the provisional conjunction of earth, water, fire, and wind. Both are unreal. What I call non-arising and non-cessation differs from that of the non-Buddhists.
Worldly phenomena are impermanent, while True Suchness is permanent. [Yet] worldly phenomena are also permanent.
Suchness is impermanent; both permanence and impermanence are mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*). All dharmas, such as the ten stages (*bhūmi*), are likewise conceptual proliferations.
Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), whereas Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not.
Yet, in the eighth stage, there is no further extinction of sensation. Is it attained or not attained by one who realizes this? It is like crossing water in a dream.
Before crossing over, one awakens. Having awakened, one reflects upon whether [this state] is correct or inverted. One speaks of the dharmas of the ten stages through false conceptualization;
yet within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no characteristic of sequential continuity, nor do the dharmas of the ten stages exist as such.

What is false? What is false conceptualization? The ground of abiding in ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) coexists with the seven consciousnesses, like the waves of the ocean, constantly flowing on without end.
It is severed. However, this is the source of the *ālayavijñāna*, the pure *amala-vijñāna*. It is the white-pure consciousness (*śukla-vijñāna*), which is also the *ādāna-vijñāna*.
It is neither discriminative nor non-discriminative; within it there is neither reality nor emptiness. This is called suchness (*tathatā*).
Already transformed! He is not me; I am truly he. Only by understanding it thus can one accord with suchness (*tathatā*).
When Dongshan met "Him" while crossing the water, what kind of realm was that? Old Master Bodhidharma’s teeth were no longer subject to the wind.

The sands of the Ganges that I speak of are not sands; what I call sands are not sands. What I call a metaphor is not a metaphor. Have you all understood this?
All phenomena are unarisen; this is what is meant by the meaning of "moment" (*kṣaṇa*). In a single moment there are nine hundred arisings and ceasings.
Within one thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) there are ninety moments. In one day and night there are six million four hundred and eighty thousand moments.
Moment by moment, thought after thought, they change and perish. Nevertheless, although it is thus, "moment" is but a concealed designation; a moment is not [ultimately real].
A single *kṣaṇa*. Yet this is something that all ordinary, ignorant people cannot perceive. An ancient said:
"When one departs in a single *kṣaṇa*, how is it that he fills empty space? How does he go as to fill empty space? It is better not to go at all. Does this avoid his fault?
The six *pāramitās*, the ten *pāramitās*, and the foremost *pāramitā*—these are not, in fact, the foremost.

The Buddha’s words take the mind as their essence; no-gate is the dharma-gate. Those who enter through a gate do not possess the family treasure.
How does one enter here? [He] throws down his staff, looks left and right, and says: "The King of Laṅkā has passed by."

Preface by Weimo of Yunxi:
Vimalakīrti’s single silence suddenly awakened the thirty-two meanings; at that moment, the radiance was like a blazing flame. He remained silent, yet he preceded Vimalakīrti.
Already there has been no small amount of leakage. Where else could there be room for further prolixity? Nevertheless, speaking is silence, and silence is speaking.
The broad and long tongues of the thirty-two great beings are all contained within the mouth of Vimalakīrti;
yet the broad and long tongue of the layman Vimalakīrti is, in turn, within the mouth of my teacher, Layman Lingting. Therefore, while other sutras contain esoteric words, this sutra...
There is no secret language. Having finished reciting the *dhāraṇī* while remaining silent, the Master Lingyan has clarified the Way for me.
Do you understand? Do you understand? Two mouths with but one tongue. My Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive. Read this compilation!
It may be called esoteric speech; it may be called loquaciousness; it may be called silence.

Shutting his room in Magadha, sealing his mouth at Vaiśālī—these two old fellows share the same nostrils. Together we shall lift up this broken sand-pot.
He particularly wishes to borrow it from the Āmra-vana grove; exerting himself, he brings forth a host of crafty heads.
Mañjuśrī and Ajita—the fifty-two young ones of the forest—rubbing palms and grinding fists, they strive toward it with all their might.
One step forward. In the ordinary course of putting on clothes and eating meals, the twelve hundred and fifty [disciples] have all slipped away at once.
Their eyes are quick to see; their hands are quick to act. When Xuansha arrived at Putian, there were many various performances, such as fish and dragons butting horns.
He asked the Elder Xiaotang about them, but he saw none of it. This is a lingering habit from the Western Capital. Swallowing a sword.

Spitting out fire—how strange and marvelous! From King Sumerudīpa and the Bodhisattva Gandhavyūha, up to the Tathāgata Akṣobhya—all are nothing more than wooden figures striking one another, made from beans scattered about;
they are illusory and unreal phenomena. To prove this, first let us perform a scene:
when the five hundred sons of the elders offered a precious canopy, what was that "precious canopy" but broken sand?
The basin: the lotus leaf is round and round like a mirror; the water chestnut is sharp and sharp like an awl.

The hundreds of thousands of Buddhas of the three thousand great thousandfold world-system all enter together into this precious canopy—how strange this is not! A needle-point, a jujube leaf, a potter’s wheel;
within the great ocean, the footprint of an ox; Mount Sumeru is like a mustard seed. All manner of clever devices have been exhausted.

Understood. But tell me, how many points of excellence are there? This old monk only knows how to look upon the founding of the Lotus Societies by Donglin and Xilin and their preaching of the Pure Land Dharma;
it truly has its origins. It is like a horned tiger—both sides win, no difference between them.
Do you know? Do you know? "When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. This is the land of eternal quiescent light, the land of true retribution and adornment.

The lands—the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages, and the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder—have all been overturned by that Brahma King with the Conch-like Topknot, who gave them a mere nudge with his hand.

These seven treasures of gold have been mixed together with hills, mounds, ravines, thorns, and rubble, pounded into a single mass, so that they can no longer be distinguished from one another. Enough, enough! It is better not to do this.
Accepting whatever little is offered according to one's means—this much is sufficient. The sentient beings of this land are stubborn and difficult to transform;
thus, the Elder Śākyamuni concealed his immeasurable power of mastery and spoke incessantly, discoursing on purity, on defilement, and on outflows.
To speak of the untainted; to speak of the false path; to speak of the true path; to speak of the conditioned; to speak of the unconditioned; to speak of the mundane;

to speak of nirvana—do not, under any circumstances, split the East and West into two separate pieces. Have you not heard it said: "The sickness of sentient beings is the sickness of the Bodhisattva"?
"I have a great illness, one that cannot be cured by the physicians of this world. Layman Vimalakīrti lies bedridden on a single couch, preaching the Dharma of impermanence, emptiness, and suffering.
How mistaken! How mistaken! The nature of the four elements returns to its source, just as a child finds its mother.
Abandoning this body of impermanence, emptiness, and suffering, why seek another Buddha-body? He is precisely me; I am not he. His head is three inches long, his neck—"

Why is this? It is because the mind is not separated by existence and non-existence, and how could emotion be divided by grasping and rejecting? Thus, the spring breeze treats a straw dog with the same care.

The verse says: Washing one’s face, one touches the tip of the nose; the eyebrows remain only above the eyes.

When the *konghou* lute is blown through to the end in the Phoenix City, pearls are scattered across the lotus canopies. What more need be said? It encompasses heaven and earth, cutting off all streams, following along with—
Waves chasing one another; a pack of wild fox spirits, each performing the funeral rites for a deceased monk.

A cow in Huaizhou eats the grain; a horse in Yizhou suffers from a bloated belly. The stone woman sings aloud; the iron man brandishes his staff. Indifferent to life and death, forgetting gain and loss;
the six sense-faculties incomplete, the seven consciousnesses not whole—how utterly free and unrestrained! *Chui chui chui*! Willow catkins and down.
The ball rolls on; pear blossoms and butterflies fly about. The dew-pillar meets with calamity; the lantern lamp incurs slander.

As for the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva of Majestic Power and Sovereignty," I have heard that principle has no direction toward which one can proceed—it is not established by constructing a principle to set up a signpost. The Way transcends form and speech—it is not suspended...
This is the way of acting spontaneously. Why? For one who has neither thought nor deliberation need not strive for universal conformity;
one who is expansive and leisurely may likewise roam freely in the clarity of the dawn. Thus, the great Peng spreads its wings without traversing the palace steps.
When Yinglong seizes the clouds, how could it be restricted by doors and gates?

I have heard that when the celestial vault is profound and unified, its reflected light accords with the sun; when its radiance is harmoniously integrated and all-pervadingly clear, it reflects and mirrors even the most subtle things.
Why is this so? When one contemplates the mind, official duties cease at the tally; when one opens to worldly affairs, all things enter its mirror.

Thus, as the earth is used for sowing and reaping, it contains the transformative radiance of all things; as the mirror receives a double brilliance, it finds leisure and ease according to the season.
I have heard it said: those who seek stillness through the reversal of turmoil are not as good as having no fixed state of stillness, for then turmoil has nothing to follow;

those who hasten toward clarity inevitably fall into obscurity, which is not as good as concealing one's clarity, for then obscurity cannot enter. Why is this? Because the Perfected Person dwells in the movement of the Way and roams with Heaven;
the Greatly Awakened speaks not, yet naturally accords with all. Thus, when songs and pipes are played in the temple, the spirit descends.
In the courtyard, the sounding of drums and bells from within the hall causes their resonance to be heard outside.
The verse says: The gate of the Bhagavān’s Nirvāṇa— Gate upon gate, the realms are distinct and clear. East, west, south, and north— A single path, level and smooth.
Peach blossoms reach the thighs; The quail comes to the courtyard. Failing to understand the matter, they toy with their own spirits. For a thousand years...
A hundred years old, dragging along a corpse-spirit, he goes straight ahead—how very alert! On the bird-path of the Mysterious Barrier, the cords of his straw sandals entangle his progress.
He strides through a thicket of brambles; he turns his body beyond the curtain of night-brightness.
Looking out from atop the heavens, who is such a person? You must believe this: that which enters through the gate is not the family treasure.
In the Chapter on Bodhisattva Vibhūṣaṇasvara, I have heard that when many are reduced to one, people fail to realize that by means of the one, the many can be observed;

and when parts are divided, they become distinct, yet people fail to realize that through these divisions, the unity is further attained. Why is this? Because when even a single *zhū* (one ounce) is accumulated, it reaches the weight of a *jūn* or a *shí*. Thus...
Their number cannot be reckoned. If one were to select them inch by inch until reaching the most minute and subtle, they would ultimately border on the void.

For this reason, Rongcheng distinguished the musical scales while exercising caution within the "circle of the center," and Linglun examined the tones while attaining perfect harmony through the resonance of the valley.

I have heard that while their movement pervades the eight directions and extends before and behind, entering entirely into the chambers [of the senses], their principle remains as vast and turbid as the four voids, traversing both the perilous and the level without treading upon any trace.
Why is this? Those who "run and walk" demonstrate my galloping;
those who are "without track or form" transcend all boundaries and limits. Thus, the utility of the carriage and the pulling of the ropes meets with the setting forth of the feet.
Wang Liang, while between his carriage wheels and horse hooves, raised his head and lost sight of Cao Fu.
I have heard that those who rush toward the Way find their feelings transformed by the single impulse; those who move in harmony with transformation do so with serene accord to the principle.
Why is this? If there is no master within, there is no means to give rise to one's resolve;

if one does not reach the further shore, there is no means to harmonize one's perspective. Therefore, the fluttering white cotton robe simply vanishes according to its own nature, and the winding ornamental headcloth likewise unravels as it meets the void.
The verse says: Six times six is thirty-six; five times five is twenty-five. Zhaozhou’s “no clouds,” Mumen’s “universal pervasion.
Huashan shakes his bell; Niu-nan performs a dance; Heyshan smashes the drum. It is laughable and it is suspicious. Xuansha’s “you tiger! “Heaven! Heaven!
When there is nothing to do, one suffers grievously. Difficult, difficult, difficult! Ten piculs of sesame seeds spread out upon a tree. Single three.
Three pairs [of verses]. The first three and the latter three. Beside the mandarin duck pillow, pearl tears flow incessantly.

As for the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Who Purifies All Karmic Obstructions," I have heard that when an object is greater than oneself, one perceives the object and doubts it; when oneself is greater than the object, one likewise perceives oneself and...
One is deluded regarding oneself. Why is this? Those who follow the traces of physical existence necessarily lack the knowledge that turns back upon the self;
those who sink into the contemplation of internal scenery cannot avoid the wisdom that is confined to a single corner. Thus, although Mengben was brave, he could not lift his own skin;
although Li Zhu possessed extreme clarity of vision, it was difficult for him to see the lashes of his own eyes.
