I have heard it said: To transcend beyond the realm of thought is to give rise to a serene and expansive state within the spiritual breast; to remain tranquil within stillness is to allow pure emptiness to prevail in the profound palace of the mind. Why is this so?
For those who turn their backs on defilement to enter awakening do not realize that awakening itself is but delusion regarding defilement;

and those who abandon existence to follow emptiness secretly fear that emptiness may still be a stagnation within existence. Thus, as wind blows upon the water, how can the illusory not be the real? As heaven is contained within the mountain...
To point toward [the truth] is itself an inversion.
For it is heard that because transformation and the transformer are without limit, one who embodies the Way must forget its mystery.

Because cessation and the ceasing are like wind blowing upon wind, as they pass through things, no fixed standard remains. Why is this so? Although my traces have been severed, those who depart from my traces are not themselves severed.
Though all anxieties have been exhausted, the one who dispatches anxiety has not yet been dispatched; thus, the reclusive man enters the night and his departing spirit follows after him.
In the twelfth month, the ice flows away, yet in spring it does not melt.

The verse says: Darkness does not nest in its chambers; light does not pass beyond the door. Though the body is locked away, it is already on the road; though the words carry the profound mystery, there is no path to follow.
To merely manifest patterns and colors is to belong to the defiled. It causes the deaf to hear and the blind to see.
How laughable are the people of this age, who learn the Tang gait at Handan! Their life-root remains unsevered as their view of self grows ever stronger.
They have overturned that great Dharma-battle between Huikeng and Weinan; they have lost their way on a forked path where the sheep were lost. The mind finds no rest and runs wild astray.
Recognizing a thief as one's own son, and calling a servant "Master.
As the Pujue Bodhisattva Chapter says:
"I have heard that those who are not confined by external things move with a natural spontaneity (*tuiran renyun*), proceeding in harmony with the Way; they have no attachments within their minds."
Thus, one forgets emotions in a state of profound stillness, and emotion merges with the ancient Way. Why is this? Because it has never been present, yet it has never been absent;
there is nowhere it goes, and nowhere it does not go. It was for this reason that the sound of axes breaking on the Eastern Mountain moved the wind and thunder.
When the Qilin was captured during the western hunt, the *Xiangzhuan* likened it to the Dipper and the Northern Dipper.

Indeed, we have heard that those habituated to narrow perspectives will surely cling to the partial while discarding the whole; those accustomed to old hearsay will take up the trivial while neglecting the great.
Why is this? For if one initiates a task, one cannot absolve others of the responsibility for its failure; yet if one merely halts, many errors are still committed.

Those who suppress it suffer its calamities all the more severely. Thus, the physician Cang Gong took pity on the depravity of their mental dispositions, while the physician Huan looked upon the source of their chronic illness and retreated in despair.

I have heard that when the spirit is submerged in the profound ultimate, neither sorrow nor joy enters its breast; when the will is stilled in the deep and subtle, neither motion nor stillness disturbs its deliberations.
Why is this? Because when resentment is obliterated, one consequently forgets one’s kin; when love is severed, there is nothing left for which to feel hatred.
Thus, the Azure Dragon lies within the moon, yet the whip that seeks to break its horns is but a weary labor; the Jade Horse gallops against the wind, yet it is not distressed.
The carriage with its prancing hooves.
The eulogy says: One ladle, one knife; one spoon, one scoop. The creator loves to seek medicine for those who are not ill—a leaking colander.
Breaking the wooden ladle. For a long time I have heard of Zhaozhou; having arrived, there is but a single rickety bridge. "Mianzhou’s aconite, Yizhou’s ginger"—truly formidable, truly formidable!
"Caoshan’s illness, Caoshan’s illness. Leaning to the left, he does not sit in the left; leaning to the right, he does not dwell in the right.
Does one who is not ill come to see the Master? This old monk has a share in seeing him.

In the Chapter on the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment, it is heard that when the spirit and will are focused, one exhausts the subtle and gathers ease; when feelings and thoughts are unified, one examines the Way and probes the profound. Why is this?

Because when the universe is in great stillness, its light penetrates; when the mind is deep and unfathomable, it is open and joyful. Therefore, the ears and eyes remain tranquil and harmonious for three months.
Sitting in forgetfulness (*zuowang*), merchants and travelers do not pass; after seven days, the cycle returns.

I have heard that because the person abides within the norms of things, the mind is sincere even without formal precepts; because the nature guards the palace court, wisdom is upright even without desire.
Why is this? It is neither internal nor external. One gathers the spirit and listens to harmony and peace—at that, and at this.

Is it not so? The Emperor is solemnly present as if descending from the left or right. Therefore, the yellow *cong* and azure *bi* are repeatedly offered at the suburban altars and the site of the earth;
the *zao*, *huo*, and *chenxing* patterns are constantly displayed in the main palace hall.

I have heard it said: By concealing the world within the world, those who allow it to dwell in ease do not toil; by directing the One Mind toward the One Mind, those who illuminate and oversee it never exhaust their light.
Why is this? When one’s physical form is entrusted to things, the things exist and I divide them among myself.

When one examines the Dao through oneself, I take the initiative and the things unite with me. Thus, the winds from the Dipper asterism and the rains from the Bi asterism—these various omens are the sovereign’s concern.
The omen for its establishment: stones fell and water-outriders flew; those who discern the categories understand the matter of embodying the source.
The eulogy says: "For whom do you toil during the ninety-day summer retreat? You cook stone tigers and beat wild sheep. Kāśyapa’s eyebrows are twelve feet long.
The banner-pole has been toppled; gradually, let us deliberate. The supreme single aperture is utterly mysterious and wondrous. Mud..."
Vajra strikes his fist; the wooden arhat leaps about; Shigan-dang laughs out loud. From the eastern wall, the gourd whispers its report:
"The monkey has burst into the ritual hall; the tiger is wearing a paper cap."
Chapter on the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha:

I have heard that when establishing discourse, one must abide in essentials rather than using words that are vast and unrestrained; when discussing matters to penetrate the subtle, how could one rely on arguments that are superficial and expedient?
Why is this so? When words transcend the common concerns of the multitude, the seventy disciples followed their guiding principles; as for the treatises that encompass...
As for the myriad capacities [of sentient beings], the five thousand characters [of the Daodejing] serve as their standard.
Thus, the Lord of the River (Hebo) gazed out at the ocean in awe from the vast Eastern Sea, and Mount Tai and Mount Liangfu stood breathless in reverence.

I have heard that Fuxi, Shennong, Yao, and Yu did not disdain to sit together on the same mat to deliberate; how could Guangchengzi of Mount Kongtong find it difficult to respond when his shadow was beheld? Why is this so?

It is because principles are no different from principle, such that the teachings of the thousand sages are realized within my own mind; and because the texts are largely ancient texts, such that the words of the multitude are unified within my own speech.

Thus, the dark tortoise entering the Luo River required nothing more than Da nao to interpret its markings, and the white horse roaming the Yellow River required nothing more than Bo He to decipher its script.
It would not trouble even Cang Jie [the legendary inventor of Chinese characters].
I have heard that because it is neither bright nor dark, it does not abide in either of the two; because it is both white and profound, it treads the Middle Way yet further loses its own function.
Why is this? Because the noble do not enter the realm of the sages, and the humble do not hasten toward the ordinary; those who are high do not maintain the True.
In humbleness, he did not turn his back on the mundane world; thus, while manifesting in the world to protect it, he once held a single scroll of scripture.
When he withdrew his form to escape into the void, not even half a fathom of fishing line could entangle him.
A verse says: "A volume of scripture, a volume of scripture! The mountains and rivers of the great earth stare with bulging eyes. Carved from the void, the dust is shed; Painted..."
The ghosts form patterns; the handle of the alms bowl weighs three jin. Green willows and fragrant grasses; the nightingale calls out "Huan" again and again at midnight.
The skull leaps up; the dragon roars from the withered tree. At midday on Tianjin Bridge, the third watch is struck.
A shell-shedding turtle walks beyond the ridges. Only fearing that Yunmen’s staff might strike the nostrils of the Celestial Emperor. Rain falls.
The Basin Tipped Over;
The Pearl Necklace of Perfect Enlightenment (Concluded);
Preface to the Questions and Answers on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra.
In the past, there was a man who read the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* and, without understanding its phrasing or punctuation, already attained a profound realization.

For him, the path of language was severed and the nature of words transcended; he did not need to seek the Ultimate Truth among the sands of the Ganges, nor seek the wondrous sound through the transmission of the brush.
Reverend Lìtíng’s wisdom was innate from birth and his thoughts were as harmonious as a tally and its seal. He upheld the true command of Mahākāśyapa and exhausted the legacy of Vimalakīrti.
The Secret Treasury: today’s Youshan and Touzi. Truly, they shall gaze upon the Milky Way to transcend words and lean against the eastern heights to let out long sighs.
The scholars of various quarters hold the refined texts of the Persian palace and pose questions like those of Ānanda regarding his *kāṣāya*.
Thus, they exercise their command to produce these compositions; the mountains, rivers, and the great earth advance toward Langye.
Exhausting its potential, this single path of Nirvana rises from the Double Peaks to complete its meaning. Profound and subtle, it gathers the sublime;

drawing from various sources and unfolding them extensively, it serves as a chisel for fellow practitioners to use in broad circulation. From this single gate of seeing one's nature through hearing sounds—
To attain the fruits of the monastic path without passing through the stages of the *saṃgha*—this is the definitive meaning; this is the ultimate and firm reality.
With palms joined in reverence, I compose this preface.
*The Questions and Answers on the Śūraṃgama Sūtra by the Junior Scholar of Xiushui,
Zeng Wangsun; Recorded at Wanshou Linting by Jingting.*
Changshui He Yuanying Ruiyin, Zeng Wangsun Daofu,
having examined the distinctions among the classifications of the teachings.

Question: Regarding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Tiantai’s classification of the teachings places it among the Vaipulya (fangděng). Xianshou’s classification deems it Perfect (yuán) while also incorporating aspects of the Final and Sudden teachings.

Those who preface the sūtra claim it possesses perfect principle and perfect practice. Is it indeed Perfect, or not? Answer: Its doctrine of cultivation and realization is definitive (lǎoyì) rather than non-definitive;
its ultimateity and solidity are absolute rather than non-absolute. Tiantai’s classification of the teachings is equal to that of Huayan and the Roshana [Vairocana] school.
That body falls into the second [category]. Since both principle and practice are perfected, they are opened as the "Final" (Zhong) and "Sudden" (Dun).

The thirty-two manifestations of the single gate of perfect penetration were proclaimed with one voice by all present at the assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Furthermore, when asked about the ten thousand practices of a bodhisattva, the answer was:

"The three—precepts, concentration, and wisdom—and their threefold advancements; such are they. The complete exposition in Magadha is also called the six perfections (*ṣaḍpāramitā*). [This concludes] the boundary-binding and upholding.
The *Mantra-samgraha* belongs to the category of cultivated capacity (*bhāvanā-śakti*). It explains the secret causes but does not exclusively focus on the recitation of mantras.

Regarding the question of the similarities and differences among the scriptural divisions (*kośa-sūtra*), the main body of the scripture is divided into five sections. From the initial invocation (*adhyeṣaṇā*) up to the ultimate nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*) constitutes the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

The section from the "Definitive Meaning" up to the "Recitation of Mantras" constitutes the Section on Cultivating the Path (*bhāvanāmārga*). The fifty-five stages constitute the Section on Realizing the Path (*sākṣātkriyāmārga*).

The establishment of the sutra title constitutes the Section on Concluding the Sutra. The subtle demonic activities within the seven realms of humans and devas constitute the Section on Aiding the Path (*anulomamārga*).

The interpretations of the two masters, Wēnlíng and Chángshuǐ, are largely the same; is this not unassailable? Answer: According to the original text, the sutra title consists of the sections on Cultivation and Realization.

Both are raised together. In the sutras, it is clearly stated that these are abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) and abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); there are those abandoned by vision, those abandoned by cultivation, and those realized through direct witness (*sākṣāt-karaṇa*).
This has already examined the mind and distinguished vision. The three categories and seven elements encompass and give forth the ten voids.

Having attained the fundamental wondrous mind, one obtains what was never before had. At this time, the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) is clear and distinct; without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one attains realization in a single lifetime. May it be so now.
Having attained the fruit, they universally deliver beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. From this point onward, one should make vows for sentient beings and vow to realize the fruit.

Pūrṇa asked again. [The Buddha] replied: "As for correct cultivation, the nature of awakening is wondrously luminous; that this luminosity of awakening becomes a fault is because one has not yet thoroughly eliminated the subtle and fine [delusions].

One can know this by examining it accordingly. The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is all-pervasive and perfectly interfused; the one and the many contain each other, the large and the small interpenetrate, and it is free from both identity and difference."
It is apart from "is not. This very "is" is itself "not-is. The entire Dharma-realm of the *Avataṃsaka* is present without remainder.

If one cultivates and realizes in this manner, what need is there for arduous toil? The pearl tied within the garment—the great sūtra shares this same intent. What else could the path of true cultivation be but this?

If you do not understand the point of this discourse, set down your mental clouds. The magnificent mansion stands before you; you must enter through its gate. To clarify this with certainty, I have made this selection.
Yuantong struck the bell and tied the knots; drawing from the side and unfolding the winding path, Mañjuśrī recited a verse that deeply entered a single gate.
The great earth, mountains, and rivers suddenly vanished—was it not thus that he attained realization in a single lifetime?

His prior awakening to the true nature (dharmatā) and his present attainment of the Dharma-eye constitute both the sudden and the gradual, with their stages perfectly distinct. Later, for the sake of future generations, he requested and applied three expedient means.

The study of the outflows (*āsrava*) takes the precepts as its foundation. Are the various merits of upholding mantras and establishing ritual altars the primary cultivation (*samyak-pratipatti*), or are they auxiliary practices (*mārga-sahāya*)?
Although the forty-four minds and fifty-five stages differ in detail from those in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, both systems clarify each other as means to realize the fruit.
The seven destinies and six realms are likewise general to other scriptures. As for the subtle demons of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), there is no need to inquire further.
He spoke for himself: "The five turbidities and the five aggregates are the root of saṃsāra. Through deluded thoughts and clinging to objects, one takes birth and death upon oneself.
To manifest as a śrāvaka and return once more to request instruction, he points out the path of practice: by not departing from seeing and hearing, one realizes entry in a single lifetime.
Thus it is, thus it is."

Regarding the inquiry on the period when the sutra was preached and the classification of the teachings into five periods: it is said that the preaching of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* occurred after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and before the assembly of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Is the fruit of Yaśodharā receiving her prediction and Dharaṇīdhara attesting to the sutra a reliable basis for this? Answer: There are two points of doubt concerning the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. First, [the matter of] Yaśodharā...

Having received the prediction of enlightenment at that assembly, he was like the King of Sovereign Supernatural Powers; how could he have entered a chamber of lust? Furthermore, following his formal prediction, he subsequently entered nirvana.

Among the remnants of the One Vehicle, why speak of the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras)? Does the Sūtra not say: "Turning the mind toward the Great [Vehicle], one’s will and practice are equal in compassion;

with a pure body held firm, one does not suffer drowning. Whether entering the realm of Māra or the Buddha, one is able to perform what is difficult to perform. As for those of the Lesser [Vehicle]...

Those who rode [the teachings] looked upon them and retreated. Only in the Piṇḍola Cave was the entire sūtra realized; at the very end, it was upheld and requested by one whose capacity was appropriate.
When the flagpole was lowered, Kāśyapa transmitted it once more. It cannot be one, nor can it be two. Is it complete, or not?
Furthermore, commentators say that what is taught in this sūtra will not all occur at the same time; for instance, there is the King Virūḍhaka who will carry out a total extermination.
To claim that Gautama was in Persia after [the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa] is likewise incorrect. Under the Bodhi tree, he contemplated for twenty-one days;

subsequently, he traveled through hundreds of cities across the years. Was this all at one time, or were they at different times? To force the meaning while being constrained by the literal text makes it difficult to seek out the subtle scriptures.

Regarding the "Inquiry into the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata," the teachings are divided into the Exoteric and the Esoteric—namely, the Sūtras and the Dhāraṇīs. This discourse on the secret cause should be understood as referring to the recitation of mantras.

The answer states: "Reverently honoring the Compassionate and Venerable One, they seek the esoteric meaning; from the ten directions, those who come to consult for resolution gather like the sands of the Ganges, all of whom say:"

Having attained the wondrous and subtle mystery herein, how could one point to the *dhāraṇī* as being the secret treasury? Question: Regarding the proclamation of the profound and abstruse, what dharma was taught?
Why did Ānanda, during the compilation, not explain it extensively? Answer: At that time, the teaching of the Dharma was heard universally throughout the ten realms.

If one engages in verbal explanations, there will already be much superfluous meaning; such is the correct principle in the land of Magadha. I further hope for your secret instruction so that I may not fall into error.
[May] jewel-light be emitted from the crown of my head.
Question: The Buddha spoke of a divine mantra from which jewel-light radiates from the crown of his head; the Great Being Avalokiteśvara spoke of the Gate of Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong-men*).

Since the light emitted by all Buddhas likewise issues from the crown, are these two [teachings] one and the same, or are they distinct? Answer: After the emission of the flying light, there were three subsequent occasions on which he emitted light:

once from the mouth (*mukha-dvāra*), once from the chest, and once from the crown of the Buddha’s head. Only in the Gate of Perfect Penetration do the lights of all Buddhas interlace and form a lattice.
The hands bestowed were non-dual and without distinction. When the transformation Buddha spoke the mantra, light emerged from the crown of his head; the manifestation of this sign was likewise so.
It is therefore named the "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa. How could this be merely coincidental?
The request for instruction through skillful means involves many gateways of initial expedients; such a winding descent of compassion is logically appropriate.

Yet, upon reaching the later stage, one transcends these to enter through a single gateway—a single gateway leading deeply into the single path of Nirvana—which seems to contradict the meaning of the earlier skillful means.
[The Master] replied: "Only the One Vehicle is real; the other two are not true. Expedient means and the City of Illusion are both mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
Once one has deeply entered a single gate, there is no further 'exiting. It is easy for the body to exit the gate, but difficult for the gate to exit the body.
Those who enter through the gate do not possess the family treasure. Do not misunderstand this."
[The Buddha] asked, "What superior sign do you see?

[Ananda] replied, "My mind and eyes are wandering; my eyes see empty flowers. [The Buddha] pointed specifically at the essence of seeing and asked, "Seeing is already apart from seeing. Is there then a duality in seeing?
He answered, "It is like a person with diseased eyes who sees a翳 (yì—a visual defect); that essence of seeing has never been afflicted by such a defect. It is merely a floating dust [of perception]."

"Does the ultimate truth have two kinds of seeing? It is revealed that this does not follow the sense organs; it is seeing without eyes. Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, there is nothing that is not the essence of seeing.
Alas, Ānanda! Your mind and eyes are at fault for giving rise to the perception of 'seeing.

The Buddha examined the cause and, through successive inquiry, realized that what is called 'seeing' is not truly seeing, for true seeing cannot be reached by such conceptualization. Like a flower in the sky suddenly vanishing, his pure eye opened. This was one great event."
How joyous! Regarding the question on the cycle of deluded thoughts:
all cycles of deluded thoughts are inexhaustible; they arise from inversion and cease through the destruction of what is firmly grasped. They are shrouded by the five turbidities.

The fetters (*paryavasthāna*) do not exist apart from the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Yet, within this context, it is further stated that there are "internal" and "external" divisions: those of pure thought ascend to heaven, while those of pure emotion fall to earth;
those with sharp thought are clever, while those with dull emotion are obtuse. Does this not imply that the term "thought" (*saṃjñā*) is not exhaustive? Answer:

Sentient beings accumulate thoughts and emotions, resulting in delusion (*viparyāsa*). They revolve through the three realms (*tridhātu*) without any prospect of escape. Whether black or white, ascending or sinking, there is no room for selective discrimination. [This concerns] the *manas*.

Grasping at and clinging to these things is profound and hidden, difficult to dissolve. Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have not yet emptied the aggregate of consciousness; their four dhyānas and eight samādhis belong entirely to a state of empty clarity.
As long as the life-faculty remains unsevered, they will continue to take up saṃsāra for themselves. Looking toward the city of Nirvāṇa, it remains ever more distant.

Question: While the discourse on the sutra was being delivered with the hall opened wide, before the explanation of the words and meanings had concluded, he suddenly extended his golden arm and spoke of *samādhi*. What is the intent of this?

Answer: This is the path of the wondrous adornment of the *Śūraṅgama-rāja*, the King of Samādhis. Although the entire sutra points toward it and contains numerous explicit references, people have missed it.
This karmic entanglement is difficult to resolve. It is like the great sun’s orb, which can shatter total darkness; like the lion’s roar, which can subdue all beasts;
like a great mass of fire, which can consume Mount Sumeru; like a vajra sword, which can sever everything.
With his arm extended, he stroked [the disciple’s] head, and at that moment, he swallowed the Western River in a single gulp.

In the "Questioning the Mind through Seven Locations," Ānanda pursues the delusion while the Tathāgata points out the error. By tracing the mind through these seven locations, it is found to have no fundamental basis;
this being so, it is like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit. Since this has been rebuked, one must ultimately determine whether this mind exists or does not exist. Answer: A monkey.
One gazes at the moon; the moon has never been absent. To grasp its reflection is an error, for the reflection is not the true moon. The clear sky is before one’s eyes, face-to-face and nothing else.
If you ask about flowers in the sky, you must be pressing upon your own eyes.

Question: Regarding the light emitted from the face-gate, it is said that the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses are both perfectly integrated and sequentially arrayed; that the dust motes of the ten directions merge to form a single realm. Since I have heard this command, I ask:
when the light is emitted from the Buddha’s crown and the great earth no longer appears, does this land shift to another quarter? Or is it otherwise?

[Question: "Is this the state of sinking into emptiness? [Answer: It is because one establishes a basis through the investigation of phenomena (*pratītyasamutpāda*). The great earth undergoes constant flux, yet its fundamental nature is pure and inherently free from arising or ceasing.
When one enters realization through perfect penetration, the accumulation of defilements is extinguished, and all conditioned characteristics naturally cease to appear.
It is like asking about the events of a dream while awake: do they have form, or are they formless?

Question: Regarding the "fundamental luminosity of the essence of consciousness," commentators identify this as the *ālaya-vijñāna*. It is said that the unarisen and undying merges with the arising and ceasing to give rise to the sense organs, the physical body, and the objective world.

Once the characteristics of consciousness manifest, its fundamental nature becomes obscured. Is this correct? Answer: The fundamental luminosity of the essence of consciousness is indeed what is called the *ālaya-vijñāna* by the commentators. It is the unarisen and undying that merges with the arising and ceasing to initiate the sense organs, the physical body, and the receptacle world. When the characteristics of consciousness appear, the fundamental nature is indeed concealed. This is so.

The *ālaya-vijñāna* is merely called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); it is not called "the essence of consciousness" (*vijñāna-essence*). Regarding the "essence of consciousness" and the "essence of vision,"孤山 (Gushan) explains them in the same way.
To claim that the *amala-vijñāna* is the "original luminosity" (*yuan-ming*) while asserting that the *ālaya-vijñāna* is the "original luminosity" is still not acceptable.
The continuous dependent origination of sentient beings in the world is fundamentally luminous and wondrous; how could it involve coming or going?

That which can give rise to all conditions remains unchanging while following conditions, and when conditions cease, that which remains follows conditions while remaining unchanging. It is inherently pure, utterly transcending all攀缘 (pān-yuan, clinging to objects).

Awakening and nirvana take this as their fundamental basis. If it were as you say—that when the characteristics of consciousness manifest, the original nature is concealed—then inverted deluded thoughts would contradict that nirvana; how then could they be pointed out as the fundamentally pure essence?
The Buddha exclaimed, "Ānanda! and asked him a question. The Buddha’s exclamation caused Ānanda to startle and withdraw from his seat. Mazu’s single shout deafened people’s ears for three days.

Are the karmic conditions of the Buddhas and Patriarchs the same or different? Answer: They are the same—a matter of the sharp edge of a blade on a point of spiritual acuity. There is the sword that kills; there is the [sword] that brings life.
The "Human Sword" is known by those who possess the eye.

When asked while raising a fist and bending the fingers, the matter of holding up the fist and pointing with the finger belongs fundamentally to Gautama; it possesses both the real and the provisional, serving as both illumination and function. [The Master] replied: "To stop the crying."
Yellow leaves cannot avoid the grandmotherly heart; when a master picks them up, he examines them with clarity. To imitate the gourd is to incur the ridicule of others;
the impoverished son has fled.
Question: The parable of the impoverished son who abandons his father appears in the *Lotus Sūtra*, whereas Ānanda’s weeping and the recounting of this event appear in the *Saṃyuktāgama*.

Therefore, one knows that the preaching of this sūtra must have occurred after the *Lotus Sūtra*. Answer: The "jewel tied within the garment" is likewise the same parable; there is no need to investigate deeply whether the preaching of the sūtras was earlier or later.
The shaking of the earth and the emission of light differ in their phrasing but point to the same meaning.

Question: Regarding the transition from one birth to another, though one abandons this life to enter the next, one has not yet escaped the cycle of saṃsāra. On the ground of non-arising and non-ceasing, it is feared that this is not the case.

Why, then, did the Persian say he had "attained what was never before attained"? Answer: The Kālīya [demon] deluded others by pointing to the non-existence after death; having heard the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, he awakened to the reality of the body.

Thereafter, he was filled with such exultation at hearing what he had never heard before that he mistakenly believed that "casting off this life to proceed to another" constitutes non-arising and non-ceasing.
He took the *puruṣa* (the conscious spirit) to be his original nature, calling a servant "lord"—ultimately a complete perversion.
To discard the ocean and seek the bubble is a question.
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all the wondrously luminous mind; the essence of the Tathāgata-garbha has been expounded almost exhaustively.

What remains unclarified that you come again to inquire? Answer: When the ocean itself becomes a bubble, the waves cannot be called water. To be addicted to conditions is to lose the mind; it is like pointing a finger at the mud.
The month has passed; within the Han-yuan Hall, one asks further for Chang’an.
Regarding the "Eight Returns" (ba-huan) inquiry into discerning vision:
if vision is already detached from vision, there is nowhere for vision to return. A single word pointing directly to the truth is swift and rare to encounter; why then do you wind your way so long?

Replying to the disciple’s words regarding the expenditure of effort: When the water recedes, the stones appear; when spring arrives, the snow melts. With shadow-grass and probing rods, one presses in layer upon layer.
Where the path of the mind is cut off, there is poverty such that there is not even space for a needle to stand. It is like emptiness merging with emptiness, or water containing water.

Question: You say that the nature of seeing is all-pervasive, reaching out to gaze upon worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Why then do sentient beings not transcend even a fraction of an inch?
Why are there such various distinctions among Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas—some perceiving the first dhyāna, others perceiving a thousand worlds? May this be heard? Answer: It is primordial clarity.
The realization of nature is profoundly far-reaching and leaves nothing remaining; the manifest differences arise from the cultivation of practice.
The full range of categories will be explained extensively later; here, the commencement of the cultivation of practice is briefly revealed.

Regarding the question of whether "nature" is not that which is perceived by non-seeing, Jiyin (Jigu) maintains that it refers to the purity of the nature of seeing; he holds that it can only be seen by the eye itself and cannot be seen by anything else. Zhongfeng maintains that it refers to non-seeing apart from objects, as its mark is fundamentally non-existent. Are both of these views correct? Answer: The explanations of principle become increasingly superior. As for the meaning of the words: 1. Jiyin’s view emphasizes the intrinsic purity of the faculty of vision itself, asserting that the capacity to see is inherent to the nature of sight and is not an object of external perception.

This aligns with the Mahāyāna teaching that the *tathāgatagarbha* is luminous and pure by nature. 2. Zhongfeng’s view focuses on the absence of objective referents. He points out that since all phenomena are empty and devoid of self-nature (*svabhāva*), there is no "mark" (*lakṣaṇa*) of seeing to be found apart from the objects of perception. This accords with the Madhyamaka perspective that ultimate reality is free from the duality of subject and object. Both perspectives are valid within their respective contexts. Jiyin speaks from the standpoint of the *ālayavijñāna*’s luminosity, while Zhongfeng speaks from the standpoint of the emptiness of all dharmas. Together, they provide a more complete understanding of the non-dual nature of reality. Thus, while they differ in emphasis, they do not contradict one another. Both are correct.
This is inconsistent. The sutra text merely says: "If one does not see, yet seeing manifests before one, how can this be called the characteristic of non-seeing?
Indeed, that which is "not seen" is beyond the reach of seeing; this principle is fundamentally clear. Seeing is not [itself] seeing, for even seeing is detached from seeing.
One must wait for the subsequent passage before this is fully revealed.
Question: Regarding the statement that "a single hair-tip contains the lands of the ten directions," what is the meaning of this?
Answer: Mount Sumeru is contained within a mustard seed; within the mustard seed is Mount Sumeru.
The large manifests within the small, and the small manifests within the large.
It is like a flower in the sky, which fundamentally does not exist.

Question: Since flowers in the sky are fundamentally non-existent, false, and unreal, while Bodhi is pure, wondrous, perfect, pervasive, and eternal—if this seeing and these perceived objects already belong to the category of flowers in the sky, how can you further say that "this seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous Bodhi"?
[The Master] replied: "Do the shifting and changing of mountains and rivers obstruct empty space? Do seeing, hearing, coming, and going disturb profound stillness?
Within the Tathāgatagarbha, these appear like reflections or flowers in the sky; it is only because of ignorant delusion that one needlessly grasps at them."
"I am the true Mañjuśrī; there is no such thing as 'this Mañjuśrī'.
Dongshan’s awakening was that "he is not me; I am precisely he. Linji held up the "true person of no station" who enters and exits through the gates of the face.
"I am the true Mañjuśrī; there is no such thing as 'this Mañjuśrī. In the various teachings and schools, the principles are suspended and difficult to penetrate.
Meeting. Answer: There is only this one month-thickness, and no second. Beyond Mañjuśrī, how could there be another Mañjuśrī? To speak in accordance with principle, a single word suffices.
As for the phantom woman who is but a detached soul—who is the illusion and who is the reality? The true person of bare flesh enters and exits at will.
Mistaking appearances for reality blinds the head; you must be most careful. Dongshan’s "Crossing the Water" and "The Canal Where We Meet"—the Precious Mirror.
The myriad layers are not the realm of the ordinary person.
Causes and conditions arise spontaneously;

the teaching of the Dharma through causes and conditions is likewise spontaneous and free from exclusion. Having been expounded since time immemorial, how can it be called frivolous discourse (*prapañca*)? Answer: It is according to what is appropriate.

Through skillful means, he did not spare his own eyebrows; like a numinous tortoise dragging its tail, he swept away his own traces. When causes and conditions harmoniously unite, all is incinerated without remainder.
Only today, as this is proclaimed, is it finally established as the definitive meaning.
Question: "Seeing the seeing is not seeing.
Originally, the nature of seeing is uniquely wondrous, true, and eternal. When one sees the seeing, why labor to depart from seeing? Answer:

"The fundamental teaching is that the essence of seeing is like a second moon. Truly, when the seeing of the seeing has been realized, it vanishes; one runs without needing to stretch one's legs and flies without needing wings."
It soars away. When one turns the hearing back upon itself, self-hearing occurs and the object of seeing and knowing vanishes; how could this be within the reach of the mind or the eyes?
Regarding the various *samādhis*, I have now heard the secret meaning of the Buddhas as commanded. Those who expound the sutras refer to these as *samādhis*, and they are also manifest.
"Distinct. What Ānanda asked still pertains to the Hīnayāna, whereas what the Tathāgata expounded belongs to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzhi).
Their expositions differ regarding the categories of calming (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā); their commentaries on the partial and the complete teachings are not uniform. Is this so? Answer:

"He turned his mind toward the Great Vehicle and fundamentally sought the Perfect Sound. Since the answer lies within the question itself, it is a vain labor to engage in further discrimination. Whether it be samādhi, or..."
"Mati" and "śamatha"—to mention either one is sufficient. The translated text is direct and concise, using these terms to encompass the entire title.
To excerpt individual phrases and seek out specific chapters is merely to chase after fragments.

Question: Regarding the shared and distinct aspects of false views based on a single object, why are they divided into "shared" and "distinct"? The grounds for creating karma are distinct and possess their own specific causes and conditions;

yet at the time of receiving retribution, one shares the same limits of measure. Is the explanation provided by the former masters truly correct? Answer: Because people are deluded and the self is deluded, it is so called.

Their sameness is such that because others perceive while I am deluded, it is called "distinction. Delusive analogies and delusive views originally belong to the category of "concomitant arising" (anuvartaka);
when these delusions intermingle with correct knowledge, they subsequently become "independent arising" (svatantra).

Regarding the question: "The seer and the conditions for seeing appear as if they were present objects," Yongming and Changshui each divided the sections differently. The two lines—"Our original enlightened awareness is a cataract upon what is seen" and "the object of that which sees"—are the points of reference.

As for "should be separated" and "should be joined," the answer is: Yongming’s approach is correct for interpreting the text in accordance with principle. How could enlightened awareness have a cataract? It is the seer and its conditions [that do].

Because it is a cataract, the text below further explains: "The perceiving of [the cataract] is the cataract; the perceiving of the conditions is not the cataract. The cataract is the cataract’s own luminosity; that luminosity does not constitute the cataract.

Although the object perceived is the cataract, the perceiving faculty has never been the cataract. The perceiving faculty is naturally free from the cataract, yet it simultaneously knows the cataract.
Did I not say previously: "To see the cataract is not the disease"? If one knows it is a cataract, the cataract does not become a disease. The two natures of light and darkness have never been two...
Question: Regarding the arising and ceasing, coming and going, which are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha—
if the arising and ceasing produced by causes and conditions all belong to mere designations and there is originally nothing within the Tathāgatagarbha— why not speak directly [of that]?

Rushing toward the unsurpassed ultimate, the aggregates, sense bases, and elements merely cause such confusion here. [The Master] replied: "I do not discard a single dharma, nor do I accept a single speck of dust.
The worldly means of livelihood do not contradict the true mark (*dharmatā*). It must be that you, O Benevolent One, have made manifold distinctions;
by clinging to these various extremes, you have given rise to attachment yourself. What does that lion’s roar have to do with the iron ox? How could a wooden man, being insentient, be startled?"
Flowers and birds.

Questions on the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). The sequence of the five aggregates is difficult to dissolve within the sphere of consciousness. The three—bases, bases, and elements—take consciousness as their foundation; they are merely consciousness.
These transformations are illusory and not real. Are consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the essence of vision one or two? Answer: Outside of water there are no waves; gold is not distinct from its ore.

It is only upon reaching the ninth consciousness that it is termed the "essence of consciousness" (*vijñāna-śuddhi*). It is not that which arises and ceases within the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). Question:

If the entire body of *tathatā* (suchness) transforms consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*), how can one discern what is illusory and what is solid? Answer: In this transformation, no emotional attachment remains.

Abundant activity exists within meditative concentration; though the Mirror-like Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) is precisely this [state], it contains all seeds. As arising and ceasing have not yet ceased, it is not called "pure white" (śukla-viśuddha).

How could the essence of the clear, tranquil ocean be something external to the floating bubbles? It is not that by recognizing the bubbles one takes them to be the vast ocean. Again he asked: "The fundamental nature of original awareness is the profound, primordial luminosity.
To blame this awakened clarity for giving rise to an object of perception (*ālambana*)—is this not the subtle essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*)? It does not transcend this.

To fully understand this: how could it be the eternally pure essence of *nirvāṇa*? Answer: The second moon is merely what appears from the single moon; it can never be called the moon itself, nor can it be considered the moon.
Because one establishes an object based on a cause (the light), that object arises falsely. How could one blame the light for this, or discard the luminous awareness?
It is like seeking moisture by churning waves; the nature of wetness is entirely absent. Not only is the wave lost, but the water itself is lost as well. Fundamentally...
To clearly perceive that the nature of seeing is fully endowed with nirvana is to see its subtle essence, free from the discrimination of seeing.
Regarding the essence of seeing and the nature of seeing:

when the two conditions of light and darkness trigger the seeing to absorb sensory objects, the nature of seeing and the essence of seeing fundamentally lack any inherent self-substance. Bodhi and nirvana...
"What is the root of the *panshui* (the six sense bases)? Answer: Did we not say later that the roots and objects share the same origin, and that liberation from bondage is non-dual?

That which was originally one refined spirit became the sixfold combination; both nirvana and birth-and-death arise entirely from the six sense faculties. Therefore, one should select one door of perfect penetration and enter deeply through it."

Question: Regarding the "harmonious conjunction of causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya-sāmagrī*), how is it divided into four meanings? Answer: "Cause" (*hetu*) refers to the past; "condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to what manifests in the present; "harmony" (*saṃ*) means there is no division between them;

"conjunction" (*gha*) means that even while they stand as two, they are united. Question: When all various causes and conditions have been eliminated without remainder, where does the Tathāgata point toward as his ultimate destination?

"What is it that will be abandoned? He replied: "The Buddha has explained the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) as being like a clear, cloudless sky, never leaving even a single film of cataract in the eye.
When the core of a plantain tree is peeled away, there is no solidity within; who among the world’s skillful illusionists could produce a real phenomenon?"

Question: Regarding the "internal objects" (*adhyātma-viṣaya*) that are apprehended—why are they called internal objects? Are they images of conceptualization (*vikalpa-pratibimba*), or are they the independent mental consciousness (*manas*) alone? Answer: When the images of external objects (*bāhya-viṣaya*) subside, they are drawn inward and absorbed.
Although they depend upon others (*paratantra*), they are for the most part produced by pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*). It is like the appearance of an image in water or within a mirror.
The moon’s form is inherently still; from whom could dust arise? Question:

The spheres of perception are illusory, and their self-nature is non-existent. Why, then, do you speak of the Tathāgata’s wondrous, true *tathatā* (suchness)? Answer: It is through thorough understanding.
The essence of falsehood is fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*). Furthermore, this wondrous true suchness has originally no self-nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the question of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): in the ultimate truth, all verbal expression is forgotten. What, then, have the Buddhas and Patriarchs ever pointed toward? Answer: The Tathāgata...
His mouth was narrow; Ānanda was deaf. Thus, at the *Śūraṅgama* assembly, he could only obtain half [of the teachings].
Question: Why did he not explain the remaining half? Answer: "The subsequent text is long; wait for another day."
The Seven Great Universal Questions:
Are these seven great universals equal in meaning? Answer: The original question concerned the four elements as a model and extended to empty space;

it cited the faculty of seeing and consciousness to investigate the ultimate, encompassing both the internal and the external, and including both the specific and the general. Question: What is the nature of consciousness and the essence of seeing?

[The text] is divided into two parts. Answer: Hearing, perceiving, and cognizing are all termed "seeing. The first five [consciousnesses] illuminate objects and possess the function of manifesting; consciousness (the sixth) additionally involves discernment, transmission, and containment.

Only when the six, seven, and eight [consciousnesses] are combined does one initially attain the complete nature. Although the principles of the preceding and succeeding [stages] differ, this does not preclude their distinct manifestation.
Question: Ultimately, what is their identity or difference? Answer: Although their substance and characteristics are distinguished, their ultimate destination is no different; they are all pervasive.

They are perfectly interfused and without duality. Question: If they are already perfectly interfused, why do they follow karma? Answer: A great thunderclap startles those at a distance, yet the deaf do not hear it;
the sun’s orb traverses the heavens, yet the blind do not see it. Though its sound resounds and its radiance shines forth everywhere, the principle remains uniform for all.
That which is neither seen nor heard is simply following one's own karma.
When the mind pervades the ten directions, one asks:
all that exists in the world is the wondrous, luminous mind. Whether it be large boulders or small pebbles, long bamboo poles or short sticks—whatever the eye beholds, let it be as it is.

The preceding [passage] should be understood according to this intent. [The Master] replied: "The radish of Zhenzhou and the cloth robe of Qingzhou are likewise all things belonging to the mundane world;
how could they be entirely identified with the wondrous mind of Bodhi? To chase after clods like a Han-lu hound is to become obstructed wherever one encounters them."
Question: Having attained the original wondrous mind, one speaks verses in praise of the Buddha;
having realized the original awakened mind, one attains verification in a single lifetime. One gives rise to great vows to again deliver beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Since this is clearly a case of sudden transcendence, how could it involve gradual progression? Answer: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is easy to understand, for it does not require passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. However, the distinctions [between the stages] are difficult to clarify; therefore, examine them further with care.
Subtle! Although the principle is realized all at once, phenomena are eliminated gradually. At the end of this scroll, the explanation shall clarify that there is no hidden intent.
Why, then, do you suddenly raise the question of mountains, rivers, and the great earth?
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth undergo successive transformations; when Avalokiteśvara’s discourse on penetration is suddenly not manifest, it may be due to the spirit...
"By force they are moved and cast to other directions; suppressed or further transmuted, they eventually perish. Answer: "That which does not manifest is pure and fundamental from the beginning;
it has never arisen, so how could it perish? As for the transmigration of beginnings and ends, these are like shadows appearing as flowers in the sky.
If the eyes do not strain, where can the flowers exist?"
Question: "If it is fundamentally pure and still, how do the mountains, rivers, and the great earth manifest as one returns home along the very path?
Answer: "The World-Honored One on that day merely used a 'probing pole' [to test the waters]. At the gate of the Patriarchs, one must face it head-on."
A single blow. Meeting face-to-face, there is no different word. To look back with hesitation is to wander a thousand miles and ten thousand leagues.

Regarding the question, "Is it that awakening is not ignorance, or is it called 'awakening-ignorance'? Wuxing says it means "awakening is entirely without ignorance. Changshui says it means "because of awakening others."
Ming: "Wenling further says that 'nature is inherently not enlightened, and one employs the mind to unite with enlightenment. I do not know which of these is correct. Answer:

To seek this too deeply is to lose the thread of the discourse. If the purport of the sutra were to say that what is called "enlightened" is because it is inherently enlightened, or conversely, that what is called "enlightened awareness" (ming-jue) is because it is not enlightened—by applying a light pressure [of inquiry] in this way, I test Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra; thus, I have set forth these two alternatives as a means of examination.

Lasso. Since ignorance (*avidyā*) deviates from the objective, it errs; it ensnares success and failure within the hook of the "Self. Based on the establishment of the object through *pramāṇa* (valid cognition), the commentary states:

"Ignorance weaves together the subject and the object. Is this indeed so? Answer: It is as you have stated. (Note: The final characters "眼施" appear to be a scribal error or fragment; they do not form a coherent part of the preceding philosophical argument.)

Gold and jade have already become too numerous as they turn green; how could one wait for dust and sand before they suffice to cause blemish and exhaustion? Since the establishment of "manifestation" (vidyā) gives rise to blame, the root fault lies in manifestation itself.
If one speaks of "ignorance" (avidyā), it is merely adding another layer of breadth.
Regarding the question: "That which is without sameness or difference is truly a conditioned dharma.
The commentary states that "that" refers to the manifest aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) as it relies upon the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

Master Wuxing further states that "without sameness and without difference" refers to what was mentioned above; that is, [the absence of] sameness and difference, as well as sameness and difference themselves.

These characteristics are collectively categorized into three. As for which of the two schools is correct regarding the existence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*): the answer is that what difference or what similarity could there be within the One True Dharma-realm?

The world and empty space are both entirely due to deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Within that which is devoid of identity or difference, there is a blazing manifestation of identity and difference;

from this, mountains, rivers, and the great earth undergo flux and change. This absence of identity or difference is the unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). That which is a blazing manifestation of identity and difference already belongs to...

There are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). Because of these, one further establishes that there is neither difference nor sameness. The four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are manifest, and conditioned existence blazes ever more fiercely.

Among dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows, none are more egregious than this. Such inverted afflictions are the fault of failing to awaken to clarity. My own narrow and limited views cannot stand before those who are truly worthy.

Question concerning the continuity of the world: The wheels of wind, gold, fire, and water are formed in succession. Logically, the wind should be at the bottom and the water should be on top. What are their respective characteristics? Answer:
According to other sūtras, the wheel of earth rests upon the wheel of water; the wheel of water rests upon the wheel of wind; and the wheel of wind rests upon space. This is the great atmosphere.
To illustrate: wind is fundamentally below; since the nature of metal is solid and obstructive, it must reside at the boundary of the wind.
There is also another wheel, like Mount Kunlun and the seven golden mountains, which does not refer to the earth. As fire rises upward, it steams moisture to become water;
when breath is exhaled, liquid condenses upon the lid of a steamer as sweat flows. Therefore, fire constantly arises within the great ocean. This is the sequence by which the world is established.

This is the fundamental nature. Question: "The clarity of awakening, the solidity of clarity, the oscillation of clarity, and the jewel-like clarity—these four wheels rely upon one another through clarity to establish their substance.

That clarity is the source of this fault goes without saying. If one discards fundamental clarity and eliminates the world, leaving only a vast, desolate, and expansive void with no place of return, would this not necessarily fall short of what the Tathāgata has affirmed? Answer: "Hills, mounds, pits, and hollows are no different from gold."
Why would the jeweled trees, banners, and pennants not be shadows of clouds? When flying light rests upon a finger, what need is there to wait for its extinction?

The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and Bodhi each form their own worlds, yet within the Tathāgatagarbha they are all-pervasive and perfectly interfused. Earth, water, fire, and wind all return to the true mark (dharmatā).
How could the deluded thoughts of transmigration be otherwise?
To clarify the principle is not to overstep [the truth].

To clarify the principle is not to overstep. The commentary asks: Is this the true, wondrous principle? The answer is: Based on the investigation of luminosity (*pratītyasamutpāda*), an objective referent is established; thus, seeing is delusion.
They mutually establish one another. It clarifies that what is known by the intellect does not exceed its proper measure: seeing does not transcend form, and hearing does not go beyond sound;
all such instances are like this. If you further claim that this is the subtle principle and true illumination, why then do you say that "awakened clarity" (jue-ming) is a fault?

Question: What is the distinction between the "seed" (*bīja*) and the "womb" (*garbha*)? Answer: The "seed" refers to the consciousness-principle (*vijñāna*), while the "womb" points to the physical form. The root of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) migrates and flows, weaving together the seed;
deluded thought (*vikalpa*) receives and integrates it, binding it into the origin of the womb. This is the beginningless, segmented consciousness-principle.
[The questioner] said: "It has already come forth; when the physical form first began to emerge from its essence, how could the outflows of conditioned habituation ever arise again?
Now that the outflows are exhausted and the great earth is submerged in tranquility, I beg you, Tathāgata, to provide a turning word on my behalf. [The Buddha] replied: "Gautama."
On that day, it was not necessary to say: "I do not see the great earth, mountains, or rivers.

When asked whether water and fire can overwhelm or extinguish one another, [the answer is] that water, fire, and empty space do not overwhelm or extinguish one another. To observe their appearances is fundamentally false; to observe their nature is fundamentally true. Furthermore, how could this be otherwise?
This explains the meaning of being perfectly pervasive. Answer: Characteristics are not external to the nature; through delusion, the true is manifested. The nature resides within characteristics;

based on the true, delusion is established. When the bamboo is dense, the stream flows; when the mountain is high, the white clouds gather. Since the Dharma-realm is fundamentally vast, why doubt its perfect pervasiveness?
Question: "Detachment is itself detachment; it is neither 'is' nor 'is not.

When the jeweled lands upon the tip of a hair and the Dharma wheels of the subtle dusts are such that self and other are not separated and the one and the many mutually contain one another—is this not the unimpeded realm of the *Avataṃsaka*?
Answer: "In the room-shuttering silence of Mahākāśyapa at Rājagṛha, there was no need for lingering thought; in the speechless stillness of Vimalakīrti, there was merely the containment of the void."
"Comparing and contrasting: 'Detached from both the affirmative and the negative; it is both the affirmative and the negative. Now, bring me your staff, old monk.

Regarding the "three conditions and three causes," Changshui (Changshui Zongze) says they refer to the auxiliary conditions for the three [unwholesome acts] of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. Furthermore, Wenglun...

That is to say: the continuity of the karmic fruits of sentient beings in the world. Master Wuxing, however, states that the three types of desire and greed clarify what constitutes the cause, which assists in the various conditions for killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. It is not yet known which of these views is correct. Answer:

The World-Honored One explicitly taught that because the three conditions for the karma of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are severed, the three causes do not arise. Taking the scriptural text as evidence, Master Wuxing’s reasoning is superior. Question: Conditions...

The "produced" (the effect) is that which is created; the "producer" (the cause) is that which creates. If the produced belongs to the former and the producer belongs to the latter, what standard is there for this meaning?

Answer: Causes and conditions arise mutually; fundamentally, there is no sequence of before and after. When attachment to the body does not arise and attachment to the mind does not function, conditions are severed and causes are extinguished.
When both subject and object are simultaneously discarded, the bodhicitta arises and the mind of arising-and-ceasing ceases.
If one asks whether using the True to dispel the delusory is not called "original suchness," [the answer is that] having illumination and having awareness both constitute obstacles. Caoxi also said:
It is said that "Bodhi has no tree. Do you mean this? Answer: The path of non-effort is fundamentally beyond names and words;
the cases of Beishou and Nanyue are merely laborious instances brought up repeatedly.
Although one obtains a great mansion, it must be entered through its gates. Regarding the question:
"The return to the source is non-dual, yet the expedient means are manifold; by which door and window should one follow the single path to Nirvana?

Answer: At every gate is Sudhana, and in every place is Maitreya. It does not require even a snap of the fingers for the multi-storied pavilions to open. How could those who have transcended all measure rely on [such means]?
Entering through the Gate:
An Inquiry on Opening the Path of Wondrous Practice of the Unsurpassed Vehicle.

Question: The sequence of the diagrams and texts for practice is perfectly clear; yet, the "direct transmission outside the teachings" seems like a shortcut that might lead to doubt. Answer: It is for two reasons.

For those who ride upon the vehicles and the multitudes of the Dharma-ending age, the gates of transformation and instruction are revealed as not being the ultimate truth. Those who study through the provisional three vehicles may transcend in a single thought;
how could they bypass the *saṃgha* and proceed without gradual stages?

The five turbidities are asked about in their sequential order. The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are the root, and the five turbidities are caused by them. Which comes first and which comes last? Answer:

Among the entries conditioned by defilement, the turbidity of form (*rūpa-kaṣāya*) is the very first; among the remnants of what has been extinguished, the turbidity of life (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*) is the very last. As for those that follow one another in rapid succession, their retribution...
[The preceding discussion has been] roughly covered. As for those whose obstructions are deep, their habitual tendencies are even more dominant.

Question: Since the five aggregates arise and perish from a lack of substantial reality, how does one revolve the turbidity to attain accord with the Tathāgata? Answer: First, one subdues [the afflictions].

The afflictions are eliminated next, followed by ignorance; one merely removes the silt and mud without discarding the water. The nature of water is inherently clear, and it becomes turbid only because of dust and soil.
If there were no dust or soil, the water would naturally be limpid and still.
Question on the Root of Affliction:
Since the arising of afflictions occurs within the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), why are two further definitive meanings established? Answer:

First, the five turbidities are cited to sever ignorance; second, the six sense faculties are selected to seek deep penetration. It is because afflictions are heavy and turbid that they constitute the greatest obstacle.
Because of the cultivation of the nature, it was commanded that the Perfect Penetration be engraved as its fundamental basis.

Question: The six sense-bases are profoundly still and perfectly luminous, and one may enter through any of them; why is the ear-faculty alone selected for attaining penetration? Answer: It is because the six are liberated.

The mutual fusion of the one and the many is supreme and wondrous. Avalokiteśvara enters into principle here precisely to respond to the capacities of beings; thus, the gate of *nirvāṇa* through the ears is particularly sublime.
[This applies to] both those abandoned by seeing and those abandoned by cultivation.

Question: The dust-like sands of ignorance differ in their coarseness and subtlety; the distinctions between what is abandoned through seeing and what is abandoned through cultivation are as orderly as a grid.

It cannot be settled in a haphazard manner within a single lifetime. Answer: When the accumulations of ignorance from kalpas are suddenly dissolved like stone armor, and when the hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates are abruptly realized like a flood of water, how could there be no one who attains realization in a single lifetime?
If it were not so, the long path of cultivation would be difficult to traverse.

Question: Regarding the mutual functioning of the six sense organs—seeing without eyes, hearing without ears, the muddy ox bellowing at the moon, and the wooden horse neighing in the wind—is thought also like this?

Answer: To measure the ocean with a conch shell only increases one’s own toil; to count the sands of the Ganges with a tally-stick will likely never reach the end. [This is] based on supernatural penetration (*abhijñā*).
To interpret it otherwise would be increasingly difficult to bear; the Buddha-dharma does not function in such a manner.
To ask "by what cause do you seek unsurpassed enlightenment?

while simultaneously denying cause and effect is to invite calamity and misfortune. That Ānanda harbored a single doubt was not due to a lack of vision. [The Master] replied: "He clung to the bridge."
Bathing is a dull matter that kills people. Do not fear falling into emptiness; falling into emptiness is not evil.

When Rāhula struck the bell and asked, he raised his staff and brandished his whisk, bringing both function and illumination into operation. Later, when Rāhula struck the bell again, he answered by following the same pattern. This is the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen).
There is no trace whatsoever of the Great Function’s rules here. Do not slander the Tathāgata by becoming the ringleader of this rebellion. I have a staff with which I would strike Rāhu;
he ought not to have been summoned and dispatched by others at that time.

Question: When all the Buddhas emit light and perform the empowerment of sprinkling light, at that time the Wondrous Dharma has never been proclaimed. How is it that the great assembly attains what they have never experienced before? Answer:
As soon as one enters the realm of verbal expression, it becomes a superfluous dharma. The cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) of the Buddhas is fundamentally invisible; it is fundamentally...
I have not heard it. Now, within this assembly, lights interlace one another as they are poured from crown to crown. The meaning of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa is clearly manifest before our faces;
it is preached in every dust mote and in every world-system, without interruption.
Question: The sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) share the same source; bondage and liberation are non-dual.
Since both birth-and-death and liberation arise entirely from the six sense organs, how can one realize and know this to manifest the Dharma of non-duality?

Answer: By hearing sound one awakens to the Way; by seeing form one clarifies the mind. Ignorance and nirvana do not differ by so much as an inch. The single word "knowing" is the root of all calamities.
At the gate of this [teaching], even the white ox and the dark-skinned slave are permitted to engage in discourse. Regarding the question:
"The *tathatā-dhātu* (the subtle essence) is constantly not revealed;
is it true or false that one portion of the *ālaya-vijñāna* is real and another portion is not real? Answer: It is both real and...
This is not truly a "two-headed" statement. Did I not say previously that "the false and the true are equally false, and that which is apart from the true is not true"?
Why then do you further entangle yourself with this meaning? The Buddha’s intent was likely this: whether one says it is true or says it is not true, both are feared to lead to delusion;
therefore, he did not expound upon them. By cutting off both extremes and departing from the characteristics of verbal expression, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is precisely *A*.
Ālayavijñāna and nirvāṇa are not two; ignorance and nirvāṇa are not dual. Question:
How can that which is not illusion produce illusion? How does the mind take hold of itself? Where is this illusion established? Answer: The nature of the mind is fundamentally...
It is neither illusion nor reality. If one clings to one's own mind, the defilements are already no small matter; how much more so to further give rise to grasping and attachment therein?
Is it not a great delusion for a thirsty deer to seek water in a mirage?

Question: When the six are resolved and the one perishes, there is neither one nor six. How can you clearly point out the sudden and gradual sequences? Answer: Since even "one" is not established, how could "six" arise?
In its essential nature, it completely transcends [all categories], and fundamentally there is no sequence. If one must choose among the six sensations...
Section on Application. The knots of the silk cords remain as they were until, following their sequence, they are all exhausted.

[The text] retreats to conceal the secret mechanism. Question: Are the secret words and the secret mechanism one or two? Answer: This scripture designates them at its head as the "Secret Cause. The secret resides in...
In your case, words and expressions fall short; withdrawing into silent reception is the foremost faculty. What I have previously set forth was already superfluous.
Kauṇḍinya and the others each spoke of their perfect penetration.

Question: Since each has realized perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna-prativedha*), there is no superiority or inferiority among them; why then is it necessary to select one and specifically practice through the faculty of hearing?

Answer: By entering deeply into a single door, the faculty of sound-hearing is supreme. All other skillful means are the great, perfectly interfused (*mahā-saṃvṛta*) nature of the seven elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen realms (*dhātu*);
these three are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha. Therefore, each of these is taught as a complete door of perfect penetration.

Question: Since the consciousness-mind is perfectly luminous and one enters the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (the perfected nature), and since all phenomena of the triple world are but consciousness and mind, why did Maitreya not adopt this as his path of perfect penetration? Answer:

Although the three natures—the *paratantra* (dependent), the *parikalpita* (imagined), and the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected)—are clearly distinct and can be categorized accordingly, they do not yet constitute the most supreme approach. While the six characteristics (*ṣaḍ-lakṣaṇa*) of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra are indeed definitive...
Regarding the School of the Lineage (Zongsheng): "The tradition of Maitreya’s gate still requires one kalpa.

[The questioner] asked: "If the six sense-faculties are fully gathered and pure mindfulness continues in succession, one shares a seat with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta in the Lotus Land. Is this Pure Land gate not indeed the Supreme Vehicle? [The Master] replied: "It depends on..."

When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is naturally purified. Having brought the six sense faculties under control, one has already realized perfect penetration. Yet, this meditative visualization still involves the inability to leave behind discursive thought;
how can it compare to the state where the object of hearing vanishes and all is realized as empty?
Question: Regarding entry into *samādhi* through hearing, reflection, and cultivation:
"reaching the ear" refers to hearing; "fixing the mind" refers to reflection; and "remedying habitual tendencies" refers to cultivation. These are called the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, hearing belongs to the three stages of worthiness (*tri-piṭaka*), reflection is judged to belong to the stage of application (*prayoga*), and cultivation is perfected in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Which of these two [interpretations] is correct? Answer: Although it is so titled...

The three types of wisdom are unified within this single gate. Since the nature of hearing is perfectly luminous, how could there be any gradual progression? Although there may be a sequence of beginning and gradual development, this refers only to the successive entry into the state of hearing;

it does not imply that the essence must be broken into segments. To propose the application of contemplation and cultivation in order to manifest the names of the three wisdoms is to lose the understanding of this single gate.

Regarding the question on "entering the stream and losing its object": before the verse on "entering the stream and achieving enlightenment," it says, "This 'entering the stream' should have no dual meaning. Answer:
According to Yunqi’s interpretation, entering the stream of the Dharma-nature is as the verse describes—turning the hearing back toward one's own nature (*svabhāva*).
Question: "When arising and ceasing have both ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one.

Is it correct to say that 'entering the stream and losing the object' is the principle of hearing the hearing; 'the exhaustion of the hearing and the heard' is the principle of not hearing the hearing;

'the emptiness of the awareness and the aware' is the principle of hearing the not-hearing; and 'the extinction of the empty and the emptied' is the principle of neither hearing nor not hearing? Answer: This explains the principles.
One immediately attains the manifestation of quiescence. What further principle is there? The questioner lets out a shout. The answer is: "This old monk is deaf. Question:

Regarding "perfuming through hearing" and "cultivation through hearing" in the *Vajrasamādhi*, "perfuming" (*xūn*) refers to habitual cultivation, and "cultivation" (*xiū*) refers to practice and realization. Since one is presently grasping at sounds and hearing, how can this be called "illusory like a phantom"? Answer: Listening is not... [text ends]

It is not by means of the ear, nor by means of sound. Illusory phenomena and illusory persons are free from emotion and cut off all designations. Only those who have traveled the same path will know it when looking at the donkey and looking into the well;
it is not something that can be reached by the sounds before one's eyes.

Question: Regarding the thirty-two manifestations, are these the thirty-two manifestations of the original Bodhisattva body the *sāmbhogakāya* (retribution body) or the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body)? Answer:
They are like the moon in water, manifesting forms in response to objects. Both the *sāmbhogakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya* are not real; they are called "like an illusion."
Question on the Fourteen Fearlessnesses:
Can it be conceived that the bestowal of fearlessness through the wondrous power of non-action arises from the mutual resonance of similar categories? Answer:

When Avalokiteśvara enters into the principle, each seeks according to its own category; the merit of fearlessness likewise responds according to its own category. Just as the eyes do not perceive water and the ears do not perceive heat, [the response is specific to its kind].
It is not moistened. Compassion can stop killing; emptiness can dissolve hardness; clarity can destroy darkness. When the root-body is perfectly pure, who acts as a go-between for thieves?
When sensory objects are entirely eliminated, what need is there to wait for non-extinction? The two wisdoms of the provisional and the ultimate form both female and male;

merit and wisdom are simultaneously perfected. One and many mutually encompass one another. This signifies that the categories of principle and phenomenon correspond to one another; therefore, it unites with sentient beings.
With compassionate longing, he asked four inconceivable questions.

His head, eyes, arms, and hands appeared in manifold forms; like an echo responding to a sound, he manifested these as a response to the invocation. This constitutes his supernormal power (*abhijñā*).

Is it so? Is it the nature of things (*dharmatā*)? Answer: Holding the name and reciting mantras both belong to the faculty of hearing. The eighty-four thousand [teachings] respond to stimuli by following sounds;
they are adorned with supreme purity, subtle and wondrous beyond measure. To attempt to deliberate upon or seek them through intellectual inquiry is certainly beyond one's reach.

Question: When the great earth, mountains, and rivers all simultaneously disappear, why do the myriad phenomena and the vast array of forms not likewise disappear? Answer: At that moment, pure jewel nets interlace their radiance;

where would the great earth, mountains, and rivers have room to remain? Question: To whom does the spontaneous chanting of the *brahmā* hymns owe its proclamation? Answer: Wondrous sounds are perfectly pervasive.
It extends throughout the ten directions. That the ear-faculty penetrates the profound mystery and accords with such principle is as it should be.

When Mañjuśrī spoke these verses and asked, "The ear-faculty enters and realizes the truth, harmonizing both with principle and with capacity; if you set aside the gateway of Avalokiteśvara, would there not be other skillful means? [The answer follows. Twenty.
The five elements manifest their perfection wherever they touch. Officially, not even a needle can pass; privately, chariots and horses may travel through. Question:
Regarding the "sage-nature original mind," how is it distinguished? Answer: Within that stage of sagehood, both the adverse and the favorable are permeated. Twenty.
